description.summary: Vitrin OS wire protocol v0 (wire version integers 1-2)

protocol.description:
The single IDL source of truth for the Vitrin OS wire protocol: the principal-facing interfaces spoken by agent clients over the core's listening socket, and the shim-facing interfaces spoken by per-app shims over a core-inherited socketpair. Both connection classes share one wire format; they differ only in authentication and dispatch table.
CONNECTION CLASSES. The class of a connection is fixed at accept time by the transport, never negotiated on the wire: connections on the listening socket ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/vitrin-0/core.sock) are principal connections; connections on a core-inherited socketpair are shim connections. Object 1 on a principal connection is vitrin_handshake; object 1 on a shim connection is vitrin_shim_session. Neither class's interfaces are reachable from the other: a message using the other class's opcodes dies as a fatal protocol error with no special casing.
FRAMING. Little-endian on the wire. Each message is one frame with an 8-byte header: object_id (u32), size (u16, whole frame including header; a declared size below the 8-byte header minimum, or a payload shorter than the size declares, is fatal "oversized" - and because the field is u16 the 65535-byte ceiling binds senders, which MUST NOT construct a larger frame, rather than receivers, which cannot observe one), opcode (u8), fd_count (u8, 0 or 1 - at most one file descriptor per message is a framing invariant; because the count is in the header, a receiver can drop any frame and still consume and close its fd without consulting the schema). Argument types form a closed set of seven: int (s32), uint (u32), fixed (signed 24.8), string, object (u32 id), new_id (u32 id), fd (SCM_RIGHTS, matched positionally). Strings are a u32 byte length followed by UTF-8 (no NUL terminator on the wire, embedded NUL forbidden), padded to 4 bytes; each string argument documents a maximum byte length, and violations are fatal "invalid_argument". There are no arrays and no 64-bit scalars in version 1.
OBJECT IDS. Object ids are per-connection u32 values. 0 is the null object (legal only for arguments marked allow-null); 1 is the bootstrap object, implicit at connect and never created by a message. Client- allocated ids MUST be strictly increasing and are never reused, in the range [2, 0xfeffffff]; the range [0xff000000, 0xffffffff] is reserved to the server and unused at every version so far (no event carries a new_id, so the server never allocates - vitrin_launcher.launched names the realm it created by string, not by a server-allocated object). When one request carries several new_id arguments, they MUST be distinct, strictly increasing in argument order, and all above the connection's allocation watermark; any violation is fatal "invalid_object". No version defines destructors: objects live for the connection, and objects derived from a grant become inert when the grant dies (requests on them are refused recoverably, never fatally). The server MAY emit events that reference an object whose grant has died; clients MUST tolerate and discard such events - this is safe forever because ids are never reused.
ORDERING. Each direction of a connection is a single ordered stream: the server processes requests in order, the client receives events in order, and ordering holds across objects within the connection. This guarantee is load-bearing: it is what makes the sync barrier, the buffer_done cookie protocol, pipelined capture pairing, and a threadless blocking client SDK correct with no additional machinery.
ERROR TAXONOMY. A failure is FATAL (the connection dies) when the client violated something it could have known - the grammar, the handshake order, or its own connection's object graph - or breached a documented per-connection resource bound (the petition-rate ceiling, the live-object cap, or id exhaustion: fatal "resource_exhausted", a denial-of-service confinement, not a semantic judgement). A failure is RECOVERABLE (an event is delivered and the connection lives) when a well-formed request's authority or target changed underneath it: consent outcome, expiry, revocation, human preemption, a granted verb's rate ceiling, or shim death. Corollary: once a grant is revoked or expired its objects go inert - requests on them yield recoverable refusals, never "invalid_object" death - otherwise human revocation racing in-flight requests would kill well-behaved agents. Fatal errors on principal connections are carried by vitrin_handshake.error and then the connection closes; shim connections carry no fatal-error message (a shim protocol violation is log-and-close: the shim is a core-spawned disposable child, and the core log is the debugging channel).
DELIVERY CLASSIFICATION. Requests are classified reply-bearing (hello, sync, request_grant, capture_frame, launch), fire-and-forget (move, button, scroll, type, attach, damage, commit, focus, set_fullscreen, selection), or structural mints (get_realm, create_surface, get_seat, get_launcher, get_layout_focus, get_layout_arrange), which are neither reply-bearing nor refusable: the request only mints an object, with no terminal event and no wire acknowledgement - a malformed mint is a fatal object-graph error, and a mint whose target is unknown or vacant surfaces that on first use, never at mint time. Every reply-bearing request receives exactly one terminal event, in request order (petition resolution excepted - see PETITION EVENT ORDERING), and such terminals are never coalesced. Refusals of fire-and-forget requests MAY be coalesced: at most one refused(rate_limited) per grant per bucket-refill window, and at most one refused per grant per (verb, code) pair until a subsequent request on that grant succeeds. The sync barrier bounds refusal discovery to one round trip.
VERSIONING. The protocol version is a single integer: the version attribute of this document and the first argument of hello. The v0 in the document family's name (vitrin-v0.xml) is the spec generation; the wire integer it carries starts at 1 (the schema forbids 0) and is 2 today. Prose that says "version 1" means this wire integer, and stays accurate about version 1 after later versions exist: a statement about version 1 is never silently a statement about version 2. The version named in hello is the negotiated version: the connection speaks exactly that version for its whole life, and messages introduced by a later "since" are not defined on it (using one is fatal "invalid_opcode"). A server accepts any offered version it implements and refuses the rest with fatal "version_unsupported"; because growth is strictly additive, a server whose maximum version is N implements every version from 1 to N - serving an older version means never emitting later-since events and rejecting later-since opcodes - so refusal means exactly that the client offered a version above the server's maximum. Downgrade is refusal, not negotiation: the server never counters with a different version and the refusal carries no supported-version hint (error.message is never machine-parsed); a newer client willing to speak an older version reconnects offering a lower integer - convergence by descending reoffer, bounded by the client's own maximum. Two versions exist: 1, and 2. Version 2 appends the realm_launch verb, vitrin_grant.get_launcher and the vitrin_launcher interface; vitrin_grant.get_layout_focus and get_layout_arrange with the vitrin_layout_focus and vitrin_layout_arrange facets; vitrin_principal.attention; and the three cross-realm clipboard messages on vitrin_shim_session (request_selection, selection, offer_selection) with the selection_status enum. Nothing was changed - every version-1 signature is byte-identical at version 2, which is what "strictly additive" means here, and this enumeration is appended to rather than rewritten whenever a since="2" message lands. A version-1 connection therefore never sees a since="2" opcode and needs no change; sending one on it is fatal "invalid_opcode". Growth is Wayland-style: new messages are appended with since attributes (opcodes are implicit document order, requests and events numbered separately from 0), enum entries are appended (values are immutable; deprecated-since marks, never removes), and a message signature is immutable forever - extension is a new message, never a changed one. A message's since names this document's version integer; an interface's own version attribute is a separate per-interface growth counter and does not gate the wire.
ENUM AND BITFIELD VALIDATION. An enum-referencing argument is strictly validated. A plain enum argument is checked by whole-value membership: a value that is not a defined entry is fatal "invalid_argument". A bitfield="true" enum argument is checked as a bitmask: any bit set outside the union of defined entry values is out-of-range and fatal "invalid_argument", while any combination of defined bits is legal. Thus request_grant's verbs accepts any combination of the eight defined verb bits (value 703) but a bit reserved for a future verb (for example value 256) is fatal. A verb bit is NOT version-gated: the bitfield is one mask, checked identically on every negotiated version, so a version-1 connection may name realm_launch and is answered "unsupported" rather than killed - which is the whole point of defining a bit before it is served. This is distinct from a policy refusal: outcome "unsupported" concerns a well-formed, in-range request the deployment declines to serve - including a defined verb bit this deployment does not serve - never an out-of-range wire value. Defining a verb bit before the core serves it is therefore not cosmetic: it converts a petition for that authority from a connection-killing fatal error into a recoverable answer.
ENUM REFERENCES. An enum attribute names the enum a scalar argument draws from. A bare name (for example "origin") refers to an enum defined on the argument's own interface; a dotted name (for example "vitrin_view.format") refers to an enum on the named interface. The code generator resolves references by this rule to build membership and mask tables.
STRING BOUNDS. Every string argument declares a maximum byte length in its summary as a "(max N bytes)" token; a string exceeding its bound is fatal "invalid_argument". The bound is machine-readable: the code generator extracts it from the summary token, the schema requires every string argument's summary to carry the token, and CI lints that it appears exactly once. A null string (legal only where allow-null is set) and an empty string are encoded identically (length 0) and are treated as equivalent - resource relies on this (null or empty both mean the whole realm).
PETITION EVENT ORDERING. resolved and vitrin_consent.state are sequenced only within their own petition's lifecycle (zero or more state events, then exactly one resolved) and do NOT participate in the cross-request "in request order" rule, because a petition's resolution waits on an unbounded human consent delay. A later sync's done reflects that earlier requests were processed and that any petition among them was registered and its consent initiated; it does NOT wait for that petition to resolve. A blocking client therefore reads resolved on its own schedule without deadlocking against an unrelated pending prompt.
SCENE AUTHORITY. Two kinds of authority over the shared scene are kept distinct, and only one of them is purchasable. ARRANGEMENT - which realm view sits where, at what size, and which one holds keyboard focus - is grant-governed, named by the layout_arrange and layout_focus verbs, so the unprivileged shell that arranges realms does so with attenuable, revocable, journaled authority rather than ambiently, and no window-management policy has to enter the core. ORDERING is purchasable by no grant, at any verb set, ever: the consent surface and the trust indicator composite above every principal's content; the core's own hit test, never a client's claimed stacking, decides which surface an input event reaches; no arrangement can occlude, fullscreen over, or resize away the consent surface; and no AGENT principal's cursor is ever composited into another principal's captured frame - the one cursor a capture may ever contain is the human principal's, and only for a grant that holds observe_cursor, which is the single carve-out and is itself grant-governed rather than free. A FIFTH ORDERING RULE joins the four the moment focus becomes purchasable: the HUMAN'S OWN physical input reaches only the realm the output is bound to. Splitting "which realm is shown" from "which realm receives the human's keys" in a scene that shows one realm at a time would let a holder make a human type into a realm they cannot see, which is focus theft in its sharpest form; so layout_focus is one act - bind the output and direct the human's input - and no verb set separates the two. An agent's injected input is not governed by this rule: it is addressed to the realm its own grant names and carries the emulated origin tag. CURSORS are core-composited for the reason the consent surface is: a realm that supplied its own pointer bitmap could paint a decoy and mislead the human about where input is going. Version 1 composites an AGENT principal's cursor, and only into human-visible output - never into any captured frame - so the ordering rule above binds the compositor now rather than vacuously. Whether a HUMAN cursor is composited depends on who owns the display: in nested operation the core composites none, because the host desktop draws it outside the realm view entirely; on bare metal, where there is no host desktop, the core draws the human's pointer itself, or the human has none. Both answers sit at the human-visible output stage, alongside the consent overlay and the trust indicator, so neither can reach a captured frame.
WHAT ARRANGEMENT CAN AND CANNOT SAY. The two layout verbs are served through two facets, vitrin_layout_focus and vitrin_layout_arrange, and between them they define exactly two requests: focus and set_fullscreen. There is deliberately no place, no resize, no raise and no stacking request AT ALL - not a request that refuses, but no request. A scene that shows one realm at a time, unstacked and unoverlapped, cannot honour them, and a granted verb whose requests the server cannot carry out is precisely the "deployment MUST NOT grant a verb it does not enforce" rule turned inside out. Growth arrives when the scene can honour it, as since-gated siblings on these interfaces, and never as a request that silently does less than its name. observe_cursor is still defined and refused "unsupported"; the verbs exist on the wire before a deployment serves them so that the model is expressible at version 1 and a petition for one is an answer rather than a connection death.

interface.name: vitrin_handshake
interface.description:
The connection-lifecycle object of a principal connection, implicit object 1 at connect: the authentication gate, the fatal-error channel, and the sync barrier. It lives for the whole connection.
Handshake state machine: CONNECTED, VERIFYING, BOUND, DEAD. In CONNECTED the only legal message is hello; a complete hello moves the connection to VERIFYING. In VERIFYING the client MAY pipeline further requests; the server queues them (bounded by ordinary transport backpressure, never an unbounded server-side buffer) and processes them only after vitrin_principal.bound is sent, which moves the connection to BOUND, the steady state. No request outside the handshake exchange itself is processed before BOUND - in version 1 the exchange is hello alone; a later version's proof-of-possession response request is part of the exchange and is processed inside VERIFYING (see the growth seams). Pipelining buys latency, never early execution: requests pipelined behind a hello that succeeds are queued and served only after bound, and if verification fails the connection dies ("auth_failed" or "version_unsupported") with the queued requests never processed. Any traffic before a first hello is fatal "pre_handshake", delivered best-effort if the frame parsed; unparseable garbage may be closed silently.
The unauthenticated phase is bounded in time: the server SHOULD impose a deployment-configurable deadline on every unauthenticated interval spent waiting on the client. In version 1 that interval is exactly CONNECTED - once a complete hello has arrived, remaining VERIFYING time is the server's own verifier latency - and a later version's proof-of-possession exchange keeps the deadline armed inside VERIFYING while the server awaits the client's response. A connection that exhausts the deadline (nothing sent, or a partial frame dribbled) is closed administratively - no error event, because nothing was violated; the close is indistinguishable from an ordinary disconnect. Every pre-BOUND death - pre_handshake traffic, refused verification, deadline expiry, unframeable garbage, backpressure - has its reason logged server-side.
The human principal has no wire presence in version 1: host input in nested mode is the implicit human, and only agents handshake.

request.name: hello
request.description:
The only pre-authentication message: credential presentation is folded into hello rather than split across an exchange, so the whole handshake is one client message and one server terminal. Presents a credential to the core's pluggable verifier and pre-allocates the principal object that a successful handshake will bind. Success is announced by vitrin_principal.bound; failure is fatal "auth_failed" or "version_unsupported". The version accepted here becomes the connection's negotiated version for its whole life (see VERSIONING). Checks run in a fixed order: frame grammar first (fatal decode errors as usual), then the version integer, then - only for a version-accepted hello - credential verification; "version_unsupported" therefore reveals nothing about the credential or the claimed identity.
The credential encoding is deliberately opaque to the wire: credential_type names a scheme (for example "static-token", "spiffe-jwt-svid", "oidc", "ssh-cert"; at most 32 bytes) and credential carries scheme-defined bytes (at most 32768 bytes), interpreted only by the verifier. identity is the SPIFFE-shaped identity URI being claimed (at most 2048 bytes, the SPIFFE-ID maximum: a 255-byte trust domain plus path). It is a routing hint; the authoritative principal identity is the verifier-canonical string later delivered in vitrin_principal.bound, never this claimed value. The wire hard-wires no scheme; this is the signature-agility hook for future credential families, and credentials larger than one frame arrive via an fd-borne sibling request in a future version. Sender-constraint is the triple of this connection, the verified credential, and SO_PEERCRED recorded at accept: a handle minted on one connection presented on another is fatal "invalid_object".
The credential is secret material: the server MUST NOT write credential bytes into logs, error.message text, or the flight recorder - at most credential_type and the byte length may be recorded.
A refused handshake is deliberately uniform on the wire (identity-probing resistance): every credential-rejection cause - unknown identity, bad token, verifier failure, SO_PEERCRED mismatch - collapses to the single fatal code "auth_failed", and the accompanying error.message MUST be a fixed phrase that neither names the cause nor echoes the claimed identity. The cause and the claimed identity are recorded in the server log only. Verification SHOULD take uniform time across rejection causes (constant-time credential comparison, identical verification work for unknown identities) so that latency does not become the oracle the message text refuses to be.
hello is legal exactly once per connection: its opcode is defined only in CONNECTED, so a second hello - in VERIFYING or BOUND - is fatal "invalid_opcode".
This signature is frozen forever.

arg.name: version
arg.summary: protocol version the connection will speak (the negotiated version); a version the server does not implement (above its maximum) is fatal version_unsupported

arg.name: identity
arg.summary: claimed identity URI, e.g. vitrin://local/agent/demo (max 2048 bytes)

request.name: sync
request.description: Requests a done event carrying the same cookie. The done event is sent only after every request received before this one has been processed and every event those requests caused has been queued ahead of it - with one exemption: petition-lifecycle events (resolved, vitrin_consent.state) wait on human consent and do not participate in the barrier; done confirms a petition was registered and its consent initiated, never that it resolved (see PETITION EVENT ORDERING). Because actuation requests are fire-and-forget and enforcement failures are events, a threadless blocking client sends its actuations, syncs, then reads until done, raising on any refused event seen - bounding failure discovery to one round trip without per-actuation acknowledgements. Valid only after bound; a cookie echo, not a callback object, so it costs no id churn.

event.name: error

description.summary: fatal protocol error; the connection closes

event.description: The connection-fatal error channel. object_id is the id of the object where the error occurred (which may be 1, this object); code is namespaced by that object's interface error enum - in version 1 the only error enum is on this interface, so all fatal codes are connection-global. message is free-form debugging text and is never machine-parsed; for "auth_failed" it is a fixed, cause-free phrase (see hello: identity-probing resistance). After sending this event the server closes the connection. Delivery is best-effort: backpressure deaths (a peer that stops reading) and unframeable streams are closed without it.

arg.name: object_id
arg.summary: id of the object where the error occurred

arg.name: code
arg.summary: error code, namespaced by the cited object's interface

arg.name: message
arg.summary: free-form debug description, never parsed (max 1024 bytes)

event.name: done
event.description: Answers sync: all requests received before the corresponding sync have been processed and their events queued ahead of this event.

enum.name: error
enum.description: Every condition here is one a correct client can never trigger; the fuzz target (hostile bytes, fd bombs, forged ids) maps every decode failure onto exactly one of these codes with a clean connection death, and error paths always close any received file descriptor.

entry.name: invalid_object
entry.summary: unknown or foreign object id, id reuse at or below the watermark, reserved-range id, or multi-new_id rule violation

entry.name: invalid_opcode
entry.summary: opcode not defined for the interface at the negotiated version, including other-class opcodes and a second hello (hello's opcode is defined only in the CONNECTED state)

entry.name: invalid_argument
entry.summary: argument decode failure: bad UTF-8, embedded NUL, string over its bound, out-of-range enum value, forbidden control character, zero verbs, malformed padding

entry.name: oversized
entry.summary: declared frame size below the 8-byte header minimum, or a payload shorter than the size declares; the 65535-byte ceiling binds senders (a u16 cannot express more)

entry.name: fd_violation
entry.summary: fd count in the header disagrees with the message signature, or unsolicited fds attached

entry.name: pre_handshake
entry.summary: traffic before a first hello on a principal connection

entry.name: version_unsupported
entry.summary: hello offered a protocol version the server does not implement - i.e. above its maximum, since additive growth means a server implements every version up to its maximum; downgrade is refusal, not negotiation

entry.name: auth_failed
entry.summary: credential rejected: unknown identity, bad token, verifier failure, or SO_PEERCRED mismatch; the cause is never distinguished on the wire - uniform code, fixed message text, detail in the server log only

entry.name: internal
entry.summary: server-side failure that poisoned the connection

entry.name: resource_exhausted
entry.summary: a documented per-connection resource bound was breached: the petition-rate ceiling, the live-object cap, or object-id exhaustion; denial-of-service confinement, not a semantic judgement

interface.name: vitrin_principal
interface.description:
The bound identity: the root of the connection's authority chain, holding exactly the authority to address realms and petition for grants. Pre-allocated by hello and live upon bound. All of the principal's grants die with the connection - version 1 has no grant persistence (restore tokens are a future version's addition).
SINCE VERSION 2 IT IS ALSO WHERE SESSION-LEVEL FACTS ABOUT THE HUMAN ARRIVE, and that is a widening of "the root of the connection's authority chain" rather than a restatement of it. The attention event below is about the human, not about this principal's authority, and it is here because its scope is the connection and this is the only object whose scope is the connection. Stated rather than left implicit: an event on this object need not be an authority fact, and a later addition that puts a second, less defensible session fact here would be following a precedent this paragraph is the record of.

event.name: bound
event.description: The terminal event of a successful handshake. identity is the canonical identity as normalized and verified by the core's verifier and recorded in the grant table - not an echo of the client's claimed string. Everything the consent prompt and the flight recorder later render about this principal derives from this verifier-owned value, never from free client text.

event.name: attention

description.summary: the human asked for their attention to move

event.description:
The human pressed the compositor's own attention key. It carries no arguments and it confers NOTHING.
WHAT IT MEANS. The human made a statement about their own input state - "my hand is off this app right now" - which withdraws a transient courtesy the server extends to a human's typing: for a short, server-chosen, single-use window, a use of layout_focus or layout_arrange by a principal this event reached is not refused "preempted". It is not a confirmation, it is not a consent decision, and it delegates no authority whatsoever. Every authority the client exercises afterwards came from a grant the human already approved. A client that provokes the press gains TIMING, never authority.
WHY IT EXISTS. Without it a human at a shell running inside a realm cannot ask that shell to change the layout: the keystroke that sends the request is itself the physical input that makes the request meet "preempted", and repeating it re-arms the window, so it is a deterministic loop rather than a race.
WHO RECEIVES IT. Only principals holding a live grant that carries layout_focus or layout_arrange. Every other client stays silent, because an unconditional event would be a free keystroke-timing oracle for every connected client. The server also does not deliver the keypress to any confined application - the key is consumed - for the same reason.
NO ARGUMENTS, AND THAT IS PERMANENT. A window length was considered and refused: signatures are immutable, the window is a server-side security parameter the server must stay free to shorten, and a client that built a timer off it would be building a retry policy that belongs nowhere. An honest client sends its already-staged request immediately and shows the "preempted" refusal if it lost the race.
NOT A PROMISE THE WINDOW IS THE CLIENT'S. Any recipient may use it and the first one to be admitted consumes it; a server cannot know which of two layout holders the human meant, and choosing would be window-management policy. Receiving this event is therefore not a guarantee that a subsequent layout request is admitted.
There is deliberately no request on this interface to ask for it, no way to observe that another principal consumed it, and no verb bit governing its delivery - a grantable "receive the human's attention key" verb would put a delegation framing on a signal that delegates nothing.

request.name: get_realm

description.summary: mint an address handle for a realm

request.description:
Creates a realm address object for a realm known by name ("realm-0" is the single well-known realm of version 1). Naming is not authority: this request always succeeds structurally, and holding a realm handle only lets the principal petition. A name that is unknown or vacant yields a handle whose petitions resolve "unavailable" - realm absence is a race, not a protocol error, because realms are dynamic in later phases.
REALM CARDINALITY. Version 1 fixes the count as well as the name: exactly one realm, "realm-0". Version 2 lifts the count to a deployment-chosen limit and keeps "realm-0" MANDATORY - a version-2 server serves it and however many further realms its operator configured or vitrin_launcher created. Keeping it mandatory is what makes the widening additive rather than merely compatible-looking: every conformant version-1 client's get_realm("realm-0") still names a realm that exists, and a version-1 connection to a version-2 server is unaffected in every respect.
The further names are not discoverable on the wire at either version. There is still no enumeration - that is a reserved since="2" seam on vitrin_realm, deliberately unbuilt - so a client learns a name from vitrin_launcher.launched or out of band, and "realm-0" remains the ONE realm name a conformant client can know without being told. A deployment at its realm limit refuses a launch "capacity"; it never refuses this request, which mints a handle for any name at all.
Two authorities name realms, and they do not overlap: an operator names TEMPLATES in the server's configuration, and the server names INSTANCES it creates from them (see vitrin_launcher.launched, whose ids are opaque). A client MUST NOT construct or predict either.

arg.name: name
arg.summary: realm name (max 64 bytes); "realm-0" is the well-known one

interface.name: vitrin_realm
interface.description:
An addressing scope for petitions: grants attach to realms, and apps launch into realms. Deliberately authority-free - the handle answers "which realm are you asking about", nothing more. Realm ids are in the protocol from day one so that later multi-realm phases add enumeration and lifecycle events to this interface instead of re-plumbing addressing.
LAUNCHING IS DELIBERATELY NOT A REQUEST HERE. Starting an app is authority, and this handle has none: a launch request on it would make holding a NAME confer the power to start a process, which is exactly what "naming is not authority" denies. Launch is instead the grant verb realm_launch, exercised through the vitrin_launcher facet minted by vitrin_grant.get_launcher, so it is consented, journaled, expiring, rate-limited and revocable like every other authority rather than an ambient property of being connected. A realm handle that names a realm TEMPLATE is what such a petition addresses; the template names the program, and the program name never crosses the wire.

request.name: request_grant

description.summary: petition for authority over this realm

request.description:
Petitions for a grant and mints, in one request, the grant handle, its consent observer, and the three authority facets (view, pointer actuator, text actuator). All five new_id arguments follow the multi-new_id rule (distinct, increasing, above the watermark). The facets are born inert: they confer nothing until the grant resolves granted, and each facet's requests are checked at use time against the grant's effective verb set at the single enforcement chokepoint - a facet whose verb was not granted refuses "not_granted" recoverably. Creation order mirrors attenuation: nothing about this petition is observable through any object the petitioner does not hold.
resource selects what within the realm; null or empty means the whole realm (the only granularity version 1 serves). The string vocabulary is type-prefixed ("surface:...", "node:...", "net:HOST:PORT") and grows by version without a new request (max 256 bytes). The net: prefix is the one whose grammar is normative rather than illustrative - it names the single host and single port an egress grant covers, admits no wildcard, no CIDR and no list, and is defined with the egress verb entry it is inseparable from (see vitrin_grant.verb). A selector whose prefix this deployment does not serve, and a net: selector that does not parse, both resolve "unsupported" rather than being widened to something that does parse. verbs is the requested verb set and MUST be non-zero (an empty petition is fatal "invalid_argument"). expiry_ms of 0 means bounded only by the persistence rung. max_event_rate is in events per second, governs observation and actuation alike, and 0 selects the server's default ceiling - never unlimited. persistence is the requested rung; the durable rungs (until_revoked, always) exist in the enum from day one but resolve "unsupported" in version 1, pending provenance verification in a later phase. verbs obeys the same rule: a bit a deployment does not serve (observe_cursor and egress everywhere; whichever others a given deployment declines) is in-range, so naming one is never fatal, and such a petition resolves "unsupported" WHOLE - the server never quietly drops an unserved bit and grants the remainder, because an agent must never believe it holds authority nothing enforces. A petition naming layout_arrange has one further admission-time answer, "layout_held", when the verb is already SPOKEN FOR for the output - by a live grant carrying it, or by another petition that is still pending for it. At most one layout holder per output, decided at admission because contention is about who HOLDS the authority rather than about one use of it. The pending half is not an implementation detail: without it two petitions could race through a human's two approvals and mint two holders, which is the state the rule exists to make unreachable, so a petition that is merely waiting really does hold the slot. Clients MUST send flags 0 in version 1; bit 0 is reserved for the one_shot constraint. flags references no enum and is deliberately not wire-validated, so a set reserved bit is not a protocol error: it resolves "unsupported" - honest refusal rather than accepted-and-unenforced. Future boolean constraints are flags bits; future value-bearing constraints (such as focus conditions) arrive as a since-gated builder request preceding this one.
Version 1 policy: pending-petition admission is capped per verified identity, across all of that identity's connections (not merely per connection - opening many connections under one credential must not multiply concurrent prompts), and the deployment additionally enforces a global ceiling on concurrent-plus-queued prompts. Excess petitions resolve "busy" (the consent-fatigue valve). request_grant is itself subject to a server-side petition-rate ceiling and a per-connection live-object cap; because every petition permanently allocates five object ids (version 1 has no destructors), a connection that breaches either bound - or exhausts the id space itself - is closed fatally "resource_exhausted", confining the denial-of-service to the offending connection rather than the whole core. A pending petition is withdrawn if the connection closes: consent is in-context, so the prompt disappears with the petitioner.

interface.name: vitrin_grant
interface.description:
The wire projection of one grant-table row (principal x resource x verbs x constraints) and the single voice of the enforcement chokepoint: every capture and every actuation under this grant is checked by one server-side function whose refusals are delivered here. Born pending by request_grant, conferring nothing; exactly one resolved event ever decides its fate. A grant that later expires or is revoked goes dead and its facets go inert - their requests refuse recoverably, never fatally.
Version 1 defines no requests on this interface; version 2 defines four, all structural mints: get_launcher, get_layout_focus, get_layout_arrange and get_egress. All five facts follow from the same rule: request_grant's five new_id arguments are frozen forever, so a sixth facet can never be co-minted and must instead be minted HERE, on the grant that authorizes it. Every later facet arrives the same way.
TWO LAYOUT MINTS, NOT ONE, and the reason is structural rather than stylistic. Each facet interface declares the ONE grant verb its every request exercises, which is what generates the single-site authority check; a combined layout facet could therefore name only one of layout_arrange and layout_focus, and the other's requests would arrive at the chokepoint with no verb to check them against. The two verbs are separately petitionable and separately attenuable - that is the whole reason focus is its own bit - so they are separately minted.
Documented growth seams for later versions, each purely additive: a release destructor (withdraw a pending petition or relinquish authority early, with the tombstone rule that clients discard events to released ids), an asynchronous revoked push event (resolved still fires exactly once, ever; refused remains the enforcement-bearing signal), attenuation (minting narrower child grants), restore tokens, and an epoch-staleness refusal sibling carrying the current epoch for compare-and-swap actuation.

request.name: get_launcher

description.summary: mint the launch facet for this grant

request.description:
A structural mint: it creates the vitrin_launcher facet through which the realm_launch verb is exercised, and nothing else. Like every structural mint it is neither reply-bearing nor refusable - no terminal event, no wire acknowledgement - and a malformed mint is a fatal object-graph error rather than an authority answer.
The facet is born INERT, exactly as request_grant's co-minted facets are: it confers nothing until this grant resolves granted with realm_launch in its EFFECTIVE verb set, and every launch is checked at the single enforcement chokepoint. Minting is therefore always legal - this request is defined for every grant whatever verbs it holds, because mint-freely-and-check-at-use is the pattern the co-minted facets already establish. A launcher minted from a grant that does not hold realm_launch simply refuses "not_granted" on first use, and a launcher minted before the petition resolves does the same; neither is a protocol error, and neither leaks anything about the petition.
Why a mint here rather than a sixth new_id on request_grant: request_grant's five new_id arguments are frozen forever, so no facet added after version 1 can be co-minted. This is the same mechanism the layout facet is documented to arrive by.
Calling this more than once on the same grant mints a second, equivalent facet. That is not a special case: no version defines a destructor, ids are never reused, and each minted object is checked against the same grant at use time, so a duplicate confers no additional authority. The per-connection live-object cap is what bounds it.

request.description:
A structural mint: it creates the vitrin_layout_focus facet through which the layout_focus verb is exercised, and nothing else. Like every structural mint it is neither reply-bearing nor refusable, and a malformed mint is a fatal object-graph error rather than an authority answer.
The facet is born INERT on exactly the terms get_launcher's is: minting is always legal whatever verbs this grant holds, because mint-freely-and-check-at-use is the pattern request_grant's co-minted facets already establish, and a facet minted from a grant that does not hold layout_focus refuses "not_granted" on first use. Neither is a protocol error and neither leaks anything about the petition. Calling this more than once mints a second, equivalent facet, which confers no additional authority for the same reason get_launcher's duplicates do not.
