request.name: get_layout_arrange

description.summary: mint the arrangement facet for this grant

request.description:
A structural mint: it creates the vitrin_layout_arrange facet through which the layout_arrange verb is exercised, and nothing else. Identical in every structural respect to get_layout_focus and get_launcher - always legal, born inert, duplicates permitted, never refusable.
A SEPARATE MINT FROM get_layout_focus, deliberately. One facet interface declares one grant verb, and layout_arrange and layout_focus must stay independently attenuable: a shell granted arrangement but not focus holds a live vitrin_layout_arrange and a vitrin_layout_focus that refuses "not_granted" forever, which is exactly the shape that separation is for.

arg.name: layout_arrange
arg.summary: the arrangement facet, born inert (confers nothing until this grant is granted with layout_arrange)

request.name: get_egress

description.summary: mint the egress facet for this grant

request.description:
A structural mint: it creates the vitrin_egress facet through which the egress verb is exercised, and nothing else. Identical in every structural respect to get_launcher, get_layout_focus and get_layout_arrange - always legal whatever verbs this grant holds and whether or not it has resolved, born inert, duplicates permitted, never reply-bearing and never refusable, and a malformed mint is a fatal object-graph error rather than an authority answer.
A SEPARATE INTERFACE, NOT A REQUEST ON THE FILESYSTEM POWERBOX, and the dialect decides that rather than taste: interface/@verb is one value per interface, so an interface declaring verb="designate_file" cannot also declare verb="egress", and its egress requests would reach the enforcement chokepoint with no verb to check them against. Same rule, same answer as the layout facet, which is two interfaces for exactly this reason (see get_layout_arrange). An earlier plan row anticipated one powerbox carrying request_file, request_dir AND request_connect; the dialect cannot express it.
THE USE THIS MINTS CANNOT SUCCEED ANYWHERE TODAY, and that is a property of every deployment rather than of some. egress is refused unsupported by every deployment (see the verb enum), so no grant can resolve granted carrying it, so every request_connect through every facet minted here refuses not_granted. The mint is defined anyway, on exactly the terms get_launcher was defined on before any deployment served realm_launch: minting is not an authority oracle, and a facet that refuses on first use leaks nothing.
NOT IMPLEMENTED BY THE REFERENCE CORE. Stated here rather than only in the prose page, because a reader of this document would otherwise reasonably infer that the shipped vitrind answers this opcode as described above. It does not: its grant-object dispatch has no arm for this request, so the opcode is answered invalid_opcode and the connection dies - which is what "always legal, never refusable" is written against. The gap belongs to P2.7.3, which lands the core half together with the proxy.

arg.name: egress
arg.summary: the egress facet, born inert (confers nothing until this grant is granted with egress, which no deployment does yet)

event.name: resolved
event.description: Sent exactly once per grant, ever: the terminal event of the pending phase, after the consent decision (or policy decision) completes. On outcome granted, the remaining arguments carry the EFFECTIVE authority - the verb set, persistence rung, and expiry the human actually chose, which may be narrower than requested (Allow-once versus Allow-while-running changes the lifetime). On any other outcome the trailing arguments are zero. The effective max_event_rate is deliberately not echoed here: an agent discovers throttling operationally, through refused(rate_limited) and its retry_after_ms hint. Denial and timeout are clean distinct events, never a hang and never a connection death.

arg.name: expiry_ms
arg.summary: effective lifetime in milliseconds; 0 = bounded by the rung

event.name: refused

description.summary: the chokepoint refused one use of this grant

event.description: The single recoverable-error event for grant use, covering capture and actuation alike - one chokepoint, one refusal voice. verb names the verb whose use was refused, which also identifies the facet. For the reply-bearing capture_frame this event is that capture's terminal (exactly one of frame_ready or refused per capture, in request order, never coalesced). For fire-and-forget actuations refusals may be coalesced per the delivery classification. retry_after_ms is greater than zero only for rate_limited and hints when the token bucket refills.

arg.name: verb
arg.summary: the verb whose use was refused

arg.name: retry_after_ms
arg.summary: refill hint in milliseconds; nonzero only for rate_limited

enum.name: verb
enum.description:
The verb bitfield. Later phases append entries (key actuation, credential presentation, subtree reads) without touching existing bits, whose values are immutable. Every entry has one SDK-level dotted name, formed by replacing the first underscore of the wire name with a dot: observe, actuate.pointer, actuate.text, observe.cursor, layout.arrange, layout.focus, realm.launch, egress. The rule degenerates for a wire name that carries no underscore, and egress is the first: there is nothing to replace, so the dotted name is the wire name unchanged. Stated rather than left to be derived, because "replace the first underscore" has no answer here and a transcriber would otherwise have to invent one. The spelling is fixed here so a second implementation transcribing this enum has no name to invent.
BIT VALUES ARE ALLOCATED ONCE, REPO-WIDE, AND ARE IMMUTABLE. The gap between 32 and 512 is deliberate: 64 and 256 are reserved by allocation to verbs that have not landed yet, and reusing one later would be a permanent wire collision rather than a rename. A bit is not free merely because this document does not define it. 128 was one of those reserved bits until egress landed on it; it was taken from the allocation registry rather than chosen as the next unused-looking power of two, which is the whole point of allocating repo-wide.
DEFINED BUT UNSERVED. A verb may be defined here and refused "unsupported" by a deployment that does not serve it, exactly as the durable persistence rungs are. observe_cursor is refused by every deployment at version 2, because per-principal cursor delivery does not exist. egress is refused by every deployment too, and for a reason that is about mechanism rather than about policy: the mediating proxy a connection would be made through does not exist yet, so no deployment can enforce what the verb names. Its FACET now exists (vitrin_egress, minted by get_egress), so the reason has narrowed since the bit landed - there is a request to exercise the verb, and there is nothing behind it. layout_arrange, layout_focus and realm_launch were in that same position when they were allocated and are now SERVABLE - each has a facet interface, a chokepoint arm and prompt copy - so whether a petition for one is answered "unsupported" is a property of the deployment rather than of the wire. A client must therefore read "unsupported" as "not here, not now", never as "not in this protocol". Two reasons this staging is structural rather than cosmetic. First, an out-of-range bit is fatal "invalid_argument" and kills the connection, so a client petitioning for authority a deployment does not serve would die instead of being answered; a defined bit makes that refusal recoverable. Second, the model these bits name - cursor visibility as authority rather than display preference, arrangement as a grant rather than the shell's ambient property - is decided now and would otherwise be unstateable on the wire until a version bump. A deployment MUST NOT grant a verb it does not enforce, and a petition mixing served and unserved verbs is refused whole: narrowing a verb set is the human's move at consent time, never a silent server-side edit that would leave the agent believing it holds authority nobody checks.
Not every verb has a facet interface. observe_cursor is the ONE that has none, and it has none by construction - it widens what capture_frame composites rather than adding a request, so there is nothing for the attribute to sit on and there never will be. It was one of two until this document gained vitrin_egress; the other was egress, which was facetless only YET. layout_arrange has vitrin_layout_arrange, layout_focus has vitrin_layout_focus, realm_launch has vitrin_launcher, and egress has vitrin_egress, each a since-gated mint on vitrin_grant because request_grant's five new_id arguments are frozen forever. The layout verbs take TWO facets rather than one because a facet interface declares exactly one verb; see get_layout_arrange.
egress's facet is vitrin_egress, minted by get_egress, and it is a SEPARATE INTERFACE of its own rather than a request on the filesystem powerbox - the dialect decides that rather than taste: interface/@verb is one value per interface, so an interface declaring verb="designate_file" cannot also declare verb="egress", and its egress requests would reach the enforcement chokepoint with no verb to check them against. Same rule, same answer as the layout facet, which is two interfaces for exactly this reason (see get_layout_arrange).
HAVING THE FACET DOES NOT MAKE THE VERB SERVED, and the two are worth keeping apart because the bit's earlier refusal reason was the missing facet and that reason has now been spent. What is still missing is the out-of-core mediating proxy the connection would be made through: no deployment has one, so no deployment can enforce what the verb names, so every deployment still refuses a petition naming egress "unsupported". A granted verb with nothing behind it would be authority nobody checks.
THE net: RESOURCE PREFIX, and why it has no wildcard. egress is the one verb whose authority is not fully named by the realm: a grant that said only "this realm may reach the network" would be the blanket authority this design exists to refuse. The resource selector carries the rest, in request_grant's type-prefixed vocabulary, as "net:HOST:PORT". The grammar is WILDCARD-FREE BY CONSTRUCTION, and that is the point rather than a restriction waiting to be lifted:
- exactly one HOST - a DNS name or a literal IP address. No "*", no leading dot, no CIDR suffix, no comma-separated list. THAT THE HOST IS A DNS NAME OR AN IP LITERAL IS SPECIFIED HERE AND IS ENFORCED NOWHERE. What a parser is required to reject is the wildcard-bearing punctuation just named, plus an empty label in any position; the reference parser rejects exactly that and keeps whatever else it is handed, so net:-:443, net:user@evil.com:443, net:999.999.999.999:443 and a Unicode homograph of a real name all parse today. None of them WIDENS authority - covers is byte-exact, so no accepted selector can name more than one endpoint, which is the whole of what "wildcard-free" buys - but a homograph is a confusion attack on the HUMAN, and the task that first renders one of these strings on a consent card owns deciding the host charset before it does. Said here rather than only in the reference implementation so that both unimplemented rules in this description are labelled the same way. - exactly one PORT - a single decimal integer in 1-65535, in its canonical spelling. No ranges, no lists, no sign, no leading zero. The reason is narrower than it looks: the port is the one half of the selector a parser NORMALISES - it becomes an integer - so a non-canonical spelling would re-serialize to a different string from the one the human approved. 0443 is refused so that parse-then-re-serialize is byte-identity, NOT because the selector as a whole is canonical. Port 0 is not a port a connection can be made to and is refused. - comparison is BYTE-EXACT, case included, and the selector as a whole is therefore NOT canonical: ONE ENDPOINT CAN HAVE MORE THAN ONE SELECTOR STRING, and none of them covers another. The host is kept exactly as presented, so net:Example.com:443 and net:example.com:443 name the same endpoint (DNS is case-insensitive) and are two different selectors, and so do net:[2001:db8::1]:443 and net:[2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001]:443 (one IPv6 address has many legal literals). Both spellings of each pair parse, both round-trip byte-identically, and holding one does not cover the other. That errs narrow - the wrong answer is a refusal, never an unapproved connection - which is the only direction this comparison is permitted to be wrong in, and normalising instead would make the grant row hold a string the human was never shown. - an IPv6 literal is bracketed ("net:[2001:db8::1]:443") so the final colon that separates host from port is unambiguous. Without the brackets the selector has no parse, and no parse means the petition resolves "unsupported" rather than being guessed at. - the whole selector obeys resource's 256-byte bound like every other prefix.
A blanket egress grant is therefore not refused by policy; it is INEXPRESSIBLE. There is no syntax to abuse, which is what lets an ergonomics answer be an enumerated template rather than an allowlist language.
Because the grammar admits no wildcard, one net: selector covers exactly one other: itself. net:example.com:443 does not cover net:example.com:80 and does not cover net:sub.example.com:443. There is no subsumption to express, and a server that invented one would be widening authority a human never approved.
A NAME IS NOT THE AUTHORITY; THE ADDRESSES BEHIND IT AT GRANT TIME ARE - AND THIS RULE IS SPECIFIED HERE, NOT YET IMPLEMENTED ANYWHERE. Where the selector names a DNS name, the addresses it resolved to when the human approved are to be pinned into the grant row, and resolution is to happen only in the out-of-core mediating proxy - there is no resolver inside a realm to route around. The proxy asks the enforcement chokepoint per connection and holds no grant of its own, so it decides nothing; a connection to an address the pin does not contain is outside what was approved and is to be refused "not_granted", including a literal-IP connection under a name-scoped grant. That is what makes a DNS rebind lose rather than win by outlasting a process. No deployment obeys any of this today: the proxy and the resolver do not exist, and the grant row's pinned-address column is present-but-null by construction. The rule is stated in this document because the column and the proxy are BUILT TO it, and a reader must not read it as a behaviour anything currently has.
COMPOSITION. observe_cursor is meaningful only alongside observe. It widens what a capture contains, so a petition naming it without observe names no capture to widen; such a petition resolves "unsupported" rather than granting a bit that changes nothing, by the same rule that forbids granting a verb the deployment does not enforce. It is not an independent authority and is never inert-but-held. No other verb pair carries a dependency: observe, actuate_pointer, actuate_text, layout_arrange, layout_focus, realm_launch and egress are each independently petitionable. realm_launch in particular does NOT imply observe: authority to start an app is not authority to watch it, and an agent that wants both petitions for both. egress likewise implies nothing and is implied by nothing: reaching one host:port is not authority over the realm's pixels, and holding every other verb buys no packet.

entry.name: observe
entry.summary: capture frames of the granted resource

entry.name: actuate_pointer
entry.summary: inject pointer motion, buttons, and scroll

entry.name: actuate_text
entry.summary: inject Unicode text

entry.name: observe_cursor
entry.summary: capture frames that include the human principal's cursor - reading the human's attention, hence a verb and not a display preference; meaningful only alongside observe, and a petition naming it without observe resolves unsupported; another agent principal's cursor is not purchasable by this or any verb; refused unsupported in version 1

entry.name: layout_arrange
entry.summary: arrange the granted realm's view, subject to the ordering invariants no grant can purchase; exercised through vitrin_layout_arrange, which defines set_fullscreen and no other request - place, resize, raise and stacking are absent rather than refused, because a scene showing one unstacked realm cannot honour them; at most one holder per output, counting a live grant that carries this verb AND a petition still pending for it, so a second petition while either exists resolves layout_held

entry.name: layout_focus
entry.summary: bind the output to a view of the granted realm and direct input there - one act, because routing keys to a realm the human cannot see is focus theft in its sharpest form; exercised through vitrin_layout_focus; separate from layout_arrange because focus theft is at once the sharpest attack and the most legitimate need, so it must be attenuable alone

entry.name: realm_launch
entry.summary: launch the realm template this grant addresses into a new realm instance, through the vitrin_launcher facet; the template names the program and no command ever crosses the wire, so this is authority over an operator-written template rather than over an arbitrary command; bits 64 and 256 are allocated to verbs not yet defined here and were skipped rather than reused (128 was one of them until egress landed on it); refused unsupported in version 1, which cannot mint the facet at all, and by any deployment that does not serve it

entry.name: egress
entry.summary: open one outbound connection to the single host:port named by this grant's net: resource selector, through an out-of-core mediating proxy that asks the enforcement chokepoint per connection and holds no grant of its own; exercised through the vitrin_egress facet, which is a separate interface of its own rather than a request on the filesystem powerbox, since interface/@verb is one value per interface; the selector's grammar is wildcard-free, so a blanket egress grant is inexpressible rather than refused, and one selector covers exactly itself - though not every spelling of one endpoint is one selector, since the host is compared byte-exactly and kept as presented; SPECIFIED BUT NOT IMPLEMENTED ANYWHERE YET: a DNS name is to resolve only in the proxy and the addresses it resolved to at grant time are to be pinned into the grant row, so that a connection to an unpinned address is refused not_granted even under a name-scoped grant - no proxy, no resolver and no pinned column with a value exist today; the dotted SDK name is egress unchanged, the wire name carrying no underscore to replace; refused unsupported in version 1 and by every deployment at version 2 - the facet exists now, so what is missing is the proxy behind it rather than a request to ask through

enum.name: persistence
enum.description: The full ladder is defined from day one so the wire never changes shape when durable rungs arrive; version 1 accepts only once and while_running, and refuses the durable rungs "unsupported" because they are valid only with verified provenance (a later phase).

entry.name: once
entry.summary: single-use authority

entry.name: while_running
entry.summary: lives while the requesting principal's connection lives

entry.name: until_revoked
entry.summary: durable until explicitly revoked (requires verified provenance; refused in version 1)

entry.name: always
entry.summary: durable and auto-reissued (requires verified provenance; refused in version 1)

enum.name: outcome
enum.description: Petition-time results, each mapping to a distinct typed SDK error (or success). All are recoverable: a denial is an answer, not a protocol violation.

entry.name: granted
entry.summary: authority active; the event carries the effective verbs, rung, and expiry

entry.name: denied
entry.summary: the human said no

entry.name: timed_out
entry.summary: the consent prompt expired unanswered; petitioning again later is legal

entry.name: unavailable
entry.summary: the realm was unknown, vacant, or closed while the petition was pending

entry.name: unsupported
entry.summary: in-range but refused by policy: durable rung without provenance, reserved flag set, unserved resource prefix, or a defined verb this deployment or resource does not serve (an out-of-range verb bit is instead fatal invalid_argument)

entry.name: busy
entry.summary: the pending-petition admission cap for this verified identity (across all of its connections) was reached

entry.name: layout_held
entry.summary: layout_arrange is already spoken for on this output, and there is at most one holder per output; the holder may be a live grant that carries the verb OR a petition still pending for it, because two petitions racing through a human's two approvals would otherwise mint two holders - so a petition that is only waiting really does hold the slot. A distinct entry rather than a reuse of busy, whose meaning is the consent-fatigue valve, and answered at admission rather than at use because contention is about who HOLDS the authority rather than about one use of it - it never reaches a prompt, so it costs the human nothing. Retrying once the holder's grant expires, is revoked, or its connection ends - or once the pending petition resolves to anything other than granted - is legal, and this outcome is the ONLY thing the core says about arbitration: choosing between two would-be holders is window-management policy and belongs outside the core

enum.name: refusal
enum.description:
Emitted by the enforcement chokepoint on every refused use of a grant - capture, actuation and launch alike. Each code maps to a distinct typed SDK exception: NotGranted, GrantExpired, Revoked, RateLimited, Preempted, ConsentHeld, NoSurface, OperationFailed, AtCapacity.
Codes are not all reachable by every verb. no_surface answers "the realm has no live surface", which is the state realm_launch exists to leave, so a launch is never refused no_surface; preempted and consent_held are attention-shaped - they reach actuation and the layout verbs, and refuse neither a capture nor a launch; capacity concerns creating a realm and so reaches only realm_launch. A code's absence from a verb's reachable set is a property of the operation, never a promise the code is unused.
EGRESS reaches the grant-lifecycle four (not_granted, expired, revoked, rate_limited) and internal, and NOTHING ELSE. It is never refused no_surface, on exactly launch's terms and for a reason of its own: a connection is not made to a window, and a realm whose app has committed nothing may still legitimately have something to say to the network. That is a NORMATIVE exemption a server must implement, not an observation - the obvious implementation refuses every non-launch use with no live view, and egress joining that arm would be a bug. It is never refused preempted or consent_held either: both are attention-shaped, and an outbound socket neither reaches the human's realm nor is visible to the human, so a hand on the input has nothing to say about it. capacity concerns realm creation and so does not reach it. What the far end did instead of answering is not in this enum at all - see vitrin_egress.connect_failed, which exists because none of these codes can honestly carry it.
THE LAYOUT VERBS ARE REFUSED no_surface, and the asymmetry with realm_launch is deliberate rather than an oversight. Focusing a realm with no live view would bind the output to nothing, and arranging one has no geometry to arrange; both would be a successful-looking answer to a request that did nothing, where launch's whole purpose is to leave that state. They are refused preempted and consent_held too, on the same terms as an actuation: moving the human's attention while the human's own hand is on the input, or while that principal's consent prompt is up, is the actuation-shaped hazard those codes exist for.
preempted IS CONDITIONAL FOR THE LAYOUT VERBS, and only for them. A server MAY define an attention signal by which the human states that their own hand is off the input (vitrin_principal.attention, since version 2); while such a signal is live for a principal, that principal's layout_focus/layout_arrange use is not refused preempted. consent_held is never conditional in the same way, and the two actuation verbs are never exempted at all: a human's hand still mutes an agent actuating into the realm the hand is in. The consequence a client must accept is that two identical layout requests can be answered differently by server state the client cannot read - an agent reading only its own journal can no longer reconstruct why one landed and one did not.

entry.name: not_granted
entry.summary: the grant is not (or not yet) active, or the verb is outside its effective set: use while pending, through an ungranted facet, or after any non-granted resolution (denied, timed_out, unavailable, unsupported, busy)

entry.name: expired
entry.summary: the grant's expiry passed; checked on use and by a proactive timer

entry.name: revoked
entry.summary: revoked by hold-Esc, panel, or policy; effective on the very next request

entry.name: rate_limited
entry.summary: the token bucket is empty; retry_after_ms hints the refill

entry.name: preempted
entry.summary: physical human input owns the target right now

entry.name: consent_held
entry.summary: the principal's own pending petition has a prompt up; that principal's actuation is refused (never delivered to the app) until the prompt closes; other principals' grants are unaffected

entry.name: no_surface
entry.summary: the realm has no surface (its shim crashed or exited); never a stale frame

entry.name: internal
entry.summary: server-side failure during this use (renderer, memfd, delivery)

entry.name: capacity
entry.summary: the deployment is at its realm capacity, so no new realm can be created; a policy answer rather than a server-side failure, which is why it is not internal - retrying is legal once a realm exits, and retry_after_ms is 0 because the core cannot know when that will be. NOTE, a deliberate exception: every other code answers from the asking principal's OWN grant, but this one answers from deployment-wide state, so a principal holding one launch grant can poll launch and watch the answer flip - observing that SOME other principal created or exited a realm. That is a low-bandwidth cross-principal side channel, inherent to answering the question at all, and it is named here rather than left to be discovered; a deployment that cannot afford it must not serve realm_launch, because no attenuation of a launch grant removes it

interface.name: vitrin_consent
interface.description:
The prompt-visibility lifecycle of exactly one petition, visible to exactly its petitioner. Scoping is structural: this object is minted by request_grant itself, so an agent cannot name - and therefore cannot observe - consent activity for any petition it did not make. The interface deliberately carries no requests: nothing an agent sends can put content in front of the human, and everything the prompt renders is core-validated data (the verifier-canonical identity, the parsed verbs, realm, and expiry). The authoritative decision is never here: it arrives as vitrin_grant.resolved, so a blocking client may ignore consent events entirely.
The consent overlay is composited into human-visible output only; it never appears in captured frames - agents cannot watch prompts. Consent decisions are not protocol-expressible by design: the scripted-consent injector used by integration tests is a build-gated core hook, not a wire message.

event.name: state
event.description: Zero or more transitions, all delivered before the grant's resolved event: queued (the prompt waits behind another prompt or a policy decision), shown (the prompt is visible, all physical input now routes exclusively to it, and the agent knows to keep waiting), closed (the prompt is gone; the decision follows on the grant). Under an auto-approve consent policy (headless CI, explicitly flagged and loudly logged) the server may emit only closed, or no transitions at all.

entry.name: queued
entry.summary: waiting behind another prompt or a policy decision

entry.name: shown
entry.summary: visible; physical input is grabbed by the prompt

entry.name: closed
entry.summary: gone; the decision arrives on the grant

interface.name: vitrin_view
interface.description:
The observation capability onto a realm's composited framebuffer: in version 1, one view is the realm's whole view. Capture is a poll model: one request, one frame, no streaming. Minted inert by request_grant; every capture passes the enforcement chokepoint (grant alive, observe granted, rate bucket) and refuses recoverably via vitrin_grant.refused when it fails. The agent learns the view's dimensions from frame_ready; version 1 has no geometry protocol.
Observation is concurrent by design: capture never contends with physical human input or with a pending consent prompt, so the refusal codes preempted and consent_held never refuse a capture - they are attention-shaped, reaching actuation and the layout verbs - and the consent overlay is composited into human-visible output only, so a frame captured while a prompt is up simply does not contain it.
A captured frame contains no cursor except the human principal's, and that one only for a grant whose effective verb set holds observe_cursor. Otherwise a capture carries realm content alone; every core-composited cursor, like the consent overlay and the trust indicator, is drawn into human-visible output only. The two halves of that rule are deliberately unequal, and the asymmetry is the decision. AGENT-TO-AGENT is closed outright and is purchasable at no verb set, ever: an observer can never watch what another agent principal is pointing at. AGENT-TO-HUMAN is closed by default and opens only through observe_cursor, because reading the human's attention - and timing actions to it - is authority rather than a display preference, so it is bought at the grant, on a prompt the human sees, and is revocable with the grant. A per-grant verb is therefore the only "toggle" that exists, and there is deliberately no per-pair one. Version 1 refuses observe_cursor "unsupported", so no capture contains any cursor today; version 1 DOES composite an agent principal's own cursor, at the same output stage as the consent overlay and the trust indicator, so the rule binds the compositor NOW rather than vacuously and is exercised by every frame drawn while an agent is pointing. Whether a HUMAN cursor is composited depends on who owns the display, and the answer changes nothing above: in nested operation the core composites none, because the host desktop draws it outside the realm view entirely; on bare metal, where there is no host desktop, the core draws the human's pointer itself, or the human has none. Both answers sit on the same side of the same fork - the human-visible output stage, alongside the consent overlay and the trust indicator - so a human cursor can no more appear in a captured frame than a consent card can, and the observe_cursor rule above is unaffected by which backend is running. Where the core does draw that sprite it also HIDES it while a pointer constraint is active on the realm the output is bound to (vitrin_shim_session.pointer_constraint_state), which is the one case in this protocol where an app's ask changes what the human sees of their own pointer. That is precisely why the hiding is the CORE's and not the app's: the app asks, the core decides, and the core owns restoring the sprite on every path that ends a constraint. A realm that could hide the human's pointer itself could mislead the human about where their input is going, which is the same reason a realm may not supply the bitmap. Streaming capture is a deliberate deferral, not an omission: if a later version adds it, it arrives as since-gated sibling messages beside this poll pair, which stays valid forever.

request.name: capture_frame

description.summary: request one frame of the realm view

request.description:
Reply-bearing: exactly one terminal event per request - frame_ready on success or vitrin_grant.refused(observe, ...) on failure - in request order, never coalesced. Pipelining captures is legal; replies pair in order. The pairing is forced by the type system: fd arguments have no null form, so failure must be a distinct event. Captures are rate-limited by the grant's max_event_rate.
The frame carries the realm view's most recently composited content as of when the server processes this request; version 1 makes no freshness promise beyond that, and an agent observes change by capturing again. "Never a stale frame" is the no_surface rule: a realm whose surface is gone (shim crashed or exited) refuses rather than re-serving its last content, so a delivered frame always describes a live realm view.
The request deliberately carries no arguments: a capture is always the whole realm view, and the pixel format is server-chosen, announced per-frame by frame_ready. Region selection, format negotiation, or a streaming subscription would arrive as sibling messages in a later version, never as changes to this one.

event.name: frame_ready
event.description:
Exactly one per successful capture_frame. The fd is a fresh memfd containing the frame - always a copy; agents never see live buffers. Ownership of the fd transfers to the receiver, which MUST close it after use (the server closes its own copy after sending). Version 1 pixels are xrgb8888, row-major, origin top-left, little-endian, and stride equals width * 4 exactly - this pins the golden-frame tests and makes observation digests unambiguous (the digest domain is the whole buffer). The padding byte of every pixel (byte 3 of each little-endian xrgb8888 pixel, the X channel) is 0xFF exactly, so identical content yields identical buffer bytes and digests stay deterministic. width and height are always nonzero: a realm view that does not exist refuses no_surface rather than delivering an empty frame.
Memfd contract (binding whenever the dmabuf flag is unset - in version 1, always): the memfd's size is exactly stride * height bytes, and the server MUST seal it with F_SEAL_SHRINK, F_SEAL_GROW, F_SEAL_WRITE, and F_SEAL_SEAL before sending. The write seal is the mechanical form of the always-a-copy rule: a buffer still being rendered into cannot be write-sealed, so a sealed fd is provably not a live buffer, the mapping cannot be truncated or mutated under the reader, and the frame's bytes - and digest - are immutable for the fd's lifetime. The receiver SHOULD verify the size with fstat and SHOULD verify the seals with F_GET_SEALS before mapping - the immutability above is client-provable rather than taken on trust only when the seals are actually checked. Pixels are addressed only through this event's arguments, never inferred from the fd; row order follows the y_invert flag (row r begins at byte offset r * stride while it is unset - in version 1, always), and stride equals width times the announced format's bytes per pixel (width * 4 for xrgb8888, the only format captured in version 1). All contract arithmetic is exact: the equalities hold in unbounded integers, and a receiver MUST evaluate them without 32-bit wraparound (widening to at least 64 bits) - a frame that satisfies them only modulo 2^32 violates the contract.
A frame that violates this contract - a memfd whose size is not stride * height, a missing seal, a zero dimension, a stride inconsistent with the announced format's bytes per pixel (other than width * 4 in version 1), or nonzero flags in version 1 - is a server protocol violation, not a refusal: the client MUST discard the frame and close the fd, MAY close the connection, and MUST NOT attribute the failure to the grant. There is no wire message for it - version 1 has no client-to-server error channel by design, so a client's only sanction is disconnecting.
flags is always 0 in version 1; the reserved bits make a later zero-copy dmabuf handoff this same message with a flag, never a new signature. Flag bits are version-gated and there is no ignore-unknown-bits rule on this event: the server sets a bit only when the negotiated version defines its semantics, so under version 1 any nonzero flags is the contract violation above.

arg.name: fd
arg.summary: fresh memfd holding the frame; ownership transfers to the receiver

arg.name: stride
arg.summary: row stride in bytes; equals width * 4 in version 1

enum.name: format
enum.description: Values are DRM fourcc codes so the enum never diverges from the kernel's format namespace when dmabuf arrives. Shared by vitrin_shim_surface.attach. Version-1 capture always announces xrgb8888; argb8888 exists for the shim attach path, whose apps commit ARGB buffers. New formats append as new entries with immutable values, so widening either path is never a signature change.

entry.name: xrgb8888
entry.summary: 32-bit xRGB, DRM_FORMAT_XRGB8888

entry.name: argb8888
entry.summary: 32-bit ARGB, DRM_FORMAT_ARGB8888

enum.name: frame_flags
enum.description: Delivery variations of frame_ready, defined in version 1 but never set by it: the reserved bits are the seam that keeps later capture modes on this same message. When y_invert is set, rows are bottom-up - row r of the image begins at byte offset (height - 1 - r) * stride; GPU readback is naturally bottom-up, and the bit lets a later version hand a frame over without a flip pass instead of mandating one forever. When dmabuf is set, the fd is a single-plane dmabuf with the linear modifier implied - mirroring vitrin_shim_surface.attach, there is deliberately no modifier argument to fail to honor. The memfd seal contract does not apply (dmabufs cannot be sealed); in its place, the dmabuf's size - as reported by lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) - MUST be at least stride * height bytes (allocators round up, so exactness cannot hold), the receiver SHOULD verify that bound before mapping or importing, and a shorter dmabuf is a contract violation handled exactly like a memfd one. The frame is still a capture copy, never the live composite - always-a-copy is the capture model, not the transport - but on this path immutability is a server obligation rather than a client-provable property: the server MUST complete all writes to the buffer before sending and MUST NOT write to it afterwards; a client that needs provably immutable bytes (deterministic digests) uses the sealed-memfd path. The bits compose, and future bits append as new entries with immutable values.

entry.name: y_invert
entry.summary: rows are bottom-up (reserved; never set in version 1)

entry.name: dmabuf
entry.summary: fd is a dmabuf, not a memfd (reserved; never set in version 1)

interface.name: vitrin_actuator_pointer
interface.description:
The pointer-injection capability: move, button, and scroll, folded into one pointer class for version 1. All coordinates are realm-view pixels - what the agent observed in a captured frame is what it addresses; coordinates outside the view are clamped (detecting that the target moved underneath a stale observation is the epoch mechanism of a later phase). Minted inert by request_grant. All requests are fire-and-forget: failures arrive as vitrin_grant.refused(actuate_pointer, ...), coalescible, bounded by the sync barrier. A client-level click is move, button press, button release, sync. Later versions add intent-level motion (drag with duration and easing, interpolated server-side) as sibling requests; these primitives stay valid forever.
CURSOR MODEL. Each principal has exactly one virtual pointer per realm it holds pointer authority over, and this facet is that pointer's only name on the wire - move moves THIS principal's pointer, never a shared one, which is why per-principal cursors need no new agent-facing vocabulary. A principal is cursorless by construction rather than by declaration: an agent that never petitions for actuate_pointer has no pointer, the headless-fleet case costs nothing, and there is deliberately no request by which a principal declares, disowns, or hides a cursor. The absence of a hide request is a decision, not an omission: a visually distinct agent cursor is a human override, so cursor visibility is never the actuating principal's own choice.
Cursors are core-composited. A realm may never supply the pointer bitmap - vitrin_shim_surface has no cursor-surface role and will not gain one - because a realm that drew its own could paint a decoy and mislead the human about where input is going, which is the spoofing class the consent surface exists to exclude. A pointer image an app paints is ordinary content inside its realm view, never the pointer the core composites.
Version-1 limitation, stated rather than implied: the core delivers ONE shared pointer position per realm view to the shim (vitrin_shim_seat events carry origin, not principal identity). Drawing is not delivery: the core does composite this principal's own cursor into human-visible output, from a position only this principal's motion moves, and that changes nothing about what the shim is delivered. The consent grab's defensive rule - emulated motion must not relocate the position the human's hit test reads - exists only because that position is shared, and per-principal delivery deletes it. That correction arrives as since-gated sibling events on vitrin_shim_seat; nothing on this interface changes when it does, because this side of the wire is already principal-relative.

request.name: move
request.description: Moves this principal's virtual pointer to realm-view (x, y).

request.name: button

description.summary: press or release a pointer button

request.description: Presses or releases a button at the current pointer position. Button codes are Linux evdev codes (BTN_LEFT is 0x110).

request.name: scroll
request.description: High-resolution scroll on one axis; one wheel notch is a value120 of plus or minus 120.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: button released

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: button pressed

entry.name: vertical
entry.summary: vertical scroll

entry.name: horizontal
entry.summary: horizontal scroll

interface.name: vitrin_actuator_text
interface.description: The text-injection capability. Semantics are "deliver this Unicode string", never "press these keys": the payload bypasses keymaps and input methods entirely, and the delivery path (the shim's dynamically generated keymap) is an implementation detail the agent cannot observe. Minted inert by request_grant; fire-and-forget, refusals via vitrin_grant.refused(actuate_text, ...). Key chords are deliberately not expressible by agents in version 1 - that is a distinct key actuation verb reserved for a later phase.

request.name: type
request.description: Delivers UTF-8 text of at most 4096 bytes to the granted target. Normative control-character rule: a newline (U+000A) MUST be rendered as a Return keypress and a tab (U+0009) as Tab by the delivery path - this is how an agent submits a form or presses Enter after a URL. Every other control character - the rest of C0 (U+0000-U+001F), DEL (U+007F), and C1 (U+0080-U+009F), i.e. the whole Unicode Cc category - is fatal "invalid_argument": a correct client never emits them.

interface.name: vitrin_shim_session
interface.description:
The connection-lifecycle object of a shim connection, implicit object 1. Authentication is structural: the inherited socketpair is the credential, and the realm identity was assigned at fork - this protocol contains no request by which a shim sets, claims, or changes its realm identity. The shim's protocol version is pinned at spawn (the core and its shims are release-paired; there is no shim hello).
Shim connections carry no fatal-error event: a shim that violates the protocol is logged and its connection closed (named log-only conditions: invalid_buffer for geometry or fd-size lies, bad_order for damage or commit against a never-attached surface or an unknown buffer_id, already_initialized for a second get_seat). Socketpair EOF is shim death: the core survives, closes every in-flight buffer fd, and drops the realm's surface - agents' next captures refuse "no_surface". Version 1 has no restart policy.
VERSION 2 ADDS THREE CONVERSATIONS TO THIS OBJECT, and each is here for the same structural reason rather than by accumulation. The cross-realm clipboard (request_selection, selection, offer_selection) is here because the CORE is the party that asks, and it must be able to ask a shim that has done nothing but read configure - which rules out a facet, since a facet needs something to mint it. The pointer constraint (pointer_constraint, pointer_constraint_state) is here because the APP is the party that asks, and vitrin_shim_seat can carry neither half: it defines no requests at all, and every event on it ends with an origin tag naming a human's device or a principal's actuator, which a confined app is neither. The idle inhibit (idle_inhibit) is here for that second reason and one further: it is app-asked, and what it asks about is not input at all but the human's own panel, which no other interface in this protocol addresses from the app's side. So this object carries every exchange in the protocol whose asking party is not the one the interface it would otherwise belong to was built around.
THIS PARAGRAPH SAID "THE ONLY TWO" UNTIL D-042 (issue #306), and it is corrected here rather than left standing: a closed count in a normative description is the same tripwire 00-conventions.md 7.3 records going stale twice, and a third conversation makes a shipped count false. It is now written as a rule ("every exchange whose asking party is inverted") rather than as a number, so the next addition satisfies it instead of falsifying it.

event.name: configure
event.description: The core's first message on a shim connection, guaranteed to precede the processing of any shim request - the shim performs one synchronous read at startup before serving its private Wayland socket. Carries the realm identity (informational; the shim can never assert it) and the realm-view size the shim advertises to its app via its own output and window-configure machinery (the single-maximized layout). May be re-sent when the view resizes; a version-1 core may letterbox instead, but the message exists so that resize is never a protocol change.

arg.name: realm
arg.summary: realm identity assigned at fork (max 64 bytes)

request.name: create_surface

description.summary: create a surface for the app's content

request.description: Creates a surface through which the shim forwards its app's committed buffers. Version 1 composites realm surfaces with a trivial single-maximized layout, but nothing in the protocol hard-codes exactly one surface per shim.

request.name: get_seat
request.description: Creates the seat through which the core delivers input for this realm. Exactly one seat per session: a second get_seat is the log-and-close condition already_initialized. Because seat events are addressed to this shim-allocated object, input the core routes to the realm before the shim has created its seat has no destination and is dropped; a well-behaved shim calls get_seat during startup, immediately after receiving configure.

event.name: request_selection

description.summary: ask this realm for its current selection

event.description:
THE CORE PULLS; A SHIM NEVER PUSHES. This is the first half of the human's cross-realm copy gesture, and it is sent only because a human at the physical keyboard pressed the core's promote chord while the output was bound to this realm. There is deliberately NO selection_changed event: a shim that forwarded every app-side copy upstream would make every ordinary in-app copy a cross-realm event, which is an ambient channel wearing a broker's clothes. Because the core only ever asks, a realm cannot place anything where another realm could reach it, at any moment of its own choosing - which is what makes "cannot be triggered or forced by any realm" literally true rather than a design intention.
The shim answers with exactly one selection request carrying this serial. A shim with nothing to offer still answers, with status empty: silence is indistinguishable from a hung shim and would make the core wait on an untrusted peer. An answer whose serial is not the outstanding one is stale (a second gesture superseded it) and is discarded; a serial is never reused within a connection.

arg.name: serial
arg.summary: names the answer this request expects

request.name: selection

description.summary: answer request_selection with the app's current selection

request.description:
Fire-and-forget: there is no terminal event and no acknowledgement, because the human's gesture is the transaction and the core has nothing to tell the shim about it. What the core does with the answer is the human's business, not the realm's, and a shim that learned whether its bytes were accepted would learn something about another realm.
Only text/plain;charset=utf-8 crosses. A shim whose app offers no selection, or offers only other types, or offers bytes that are not well-formed UTF-8, answers status empty or wrong_type and sends no data; a selection above the byte bound answers too_large. The shim is expected to make that judgement rather than let the bound decide it: a data string past its bound is fatal "invalid_argument", which on a shim connection means log-and-close, and a human copying a large file must not kill their own app's shim. The bound is stated here and is immutable; raising it is a new message, never an edit.
mime and data MUST be empty unless status is ok, and the core ignores them in that case rather than treating a decorated refusal as data. The core validates the type against its own allow-list regardless of what this says: a shim is untrusted, and a status of ok is a claim, not a credential.

arg.name: serial
arg.summary: the serial of the request_selection being answered

arg.name: status
arg.summary: whether data follows, and why not

arg.name: mime
arg.summary: MIME type of data, empty unless status is ok (max 32 bytes)

arg.name: data
arg.summary: the selection as UTF-8, empty unless status is ok (max 61440 bytes)

event.name: offer_selection

description.summary: offer the core-held clipboard to this realm

event.description:
The second half of the human's gesture, and a SEPARATE, LATER, PHYSICAL act: the human pressed the core's offer chord while the output was bound to this realm. One gesture transfers nothing - promoting places bytes in the core's slot and reaches no other realm, offering reads that slot and never writes it - and the two chords are distinct, so no single press can do both.
The shim makes the payload its app's ordinary selection (a shim-owned data source on its own seat). It does NOT paste: the human still presses their app's own paste, exactly as the Qubes model this follows separates "move the clipboard into the target" from "paste it there". The core sends no offer with an empty slot, so receiving this always means there is something to install.
Sent to exactly one realm per gesture. The core never fans an offer out, and never sends one on the source realm's behalf: a slot promoted in a realm is not offered back to it unless the human gestures there.

arg.name: data
arg.summary: the clipboard contents as UTF-8 (max 61440 bytes)

request.name: pointer_constraint

description.summary: ask the core to lock or confine the pointer to a surface

request.description:
The confined app's ask, relayed by its shim. THE APP ASKS AND THE CORE DECIDES - the mirror of request_selection, where the core asks and the shim answers. That reversal is stated rather than left to be inferred, because a reader who carries the clipboard's direction over to this pair will read every rule below backwards. serial is minted by the SHIM here, and is strictly increasing within the connection and never reused, exactly as the core's own serials are.
ONE MESSAGE IS THE WHOLE STATE MACHINE'S INPUT. kind none is the WITHDRAWAL, so there is no separate unset message a withdrawal could race a set against, and no order in which the two could be applied wrongly. When kind is none, surface MUST be null and x, y, width and height MUST be zero; the core ignores them in that case rather than treating a decorated withdrawal as data - the same discipline the selection request states for mime and data on a refusing status.
THE REGION IS ONE RECTANGLE, and its cost is named here rather than discovered later. x and y are the region's origin in surface-local pixels and width and height its extent; width and height both zero means the whole surface, which is the null-region meaning of Wayland's own pointer-constraint vocabulary carried across without inventing a nullable rectangle type. Wayland permits an arbitrary region; this carries a rectangle, so a genuinely non-rectangular confinement is reduced to its bounding box and the app is NOT told that it was. An app needing an exact region must ask for a rectangle it can live with, or accept the widening. The coordinates are int and the extents uint rather than fixed: fixed is reserved for vitrin_shim_seat motion, and a region is not motion.
lifetime carries Wayland's own two, so a shim can honour a one-shot lock's destroy semantics without inventing a policy of its own. Nothing in this system has yet NEEDED oneshot; it is carried because a signature is immutable forever and adding it afterwards would be a whole new message.
FIRE-AND-FORGET, NOT REPLY-BEARING, and here that classification is load-bearing rather than bookkeeping. The verdict does arrive, as a pointer_constraint_state carrying this serial, but it is NOT a terminal event and the exactly-one-terminal rule deliberately does not apply: a constraint's state changes for reasons the shim never asked about - the human switched realms, raised a consent card, locked the screen - so binding the answer one-to-one to the ask would leave an app locked with no message that could ever tell it otherwise. That is the exact latch this design exists to prevent. The coalescing licence that ordinarily accompanies fire-and-forget is OVERRIDDEN in the strict direction: the core sends at most one pointer_constraint_state per transition and never coalesces two different states.
A SECOND ASK REPLACES THE FIRST. One record exists per connection; a second ask supersedes the earlier one, whose serial is answered superseded and hears nothing further.
ERRORS. A constraint this deployment will not serve is RECOVERABLE: the answer is state refused, the connection lives, and the app's own lock object is left inert - a legal Wayland state, since a compositor may decline to activate a lock, and that is what lets a refusal not wedge the app. What is fatal is unchanged decode-level ground: a surface id this connection never minted, or one at or below its watermark, is invalid_object (the shim violating its OWN object graph), and an out-of-range kind or lifetime is invalid_argument - on a shim connection both mean log-and-close. This request adds NO log-only condition of its own: an ask naming a surface that has never committed is a legitimate ask answered inactive, not a bad_order.
NAME IT pointer_constraint OR "pointer lock", never bare "constraint": in this protocol that word already means a PETITION constraint (vitrin_realm.request_grant's flags), and every identifier this pair mints carries the qualifier for that reason.

arg.name: serial
arg.summary: shim-minted; names the answer this ask expects

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: the surface the constraint applies to; MUST be null when kind is none

arg.name: kind
arg.summary: lock, confine, or none to withdraw

arg.name: lifetime
arg.summary: oneshot or persistent; ignored when kind is none

arg.name: width
arg.summary: region width; zero with height zero means the whole surface

arg.name: height
arg.summary: region height; zero with width zero means the whole surface

event.name: pointer_constraint_state

description.summary: the core's verdict on a pointer_constraint, and its running state

event.description:
The verdict AND the running state, on one message. They are not split into two because two ways to learn the same fact is how the two come to disagree. This is a SERVER DIRECTIVE, in the class configure occupies: correlated to an ask by serial, never terminal to it.
LEVEL-TRIGGERED, EDGE-REPORTED. The core recomputes each record's state from live conditions and sends this event only when that state CHANGED. Consecutive identical states are not sent, and two different states are never coalesced into one. A serial the shim does not recognise is stale - a later ask superseded it - and is ignored, the same rule request_selection states for its own serials.
A REFUSAL CANNOT WEDGE AN APP, and the reason is that the shim does nothing at all on refused. It does not destroy the app's constraint object and does not raise an error on it; it simply never sends the activation the object is waiting for. An inert lock object is a legal Wayland state, so the app's own state machine handles a refusal with no behaviour specific to this system.
WHAT ACTIVE MEANS FOR THE HUMAN, stated on the wire because an app must not have to discover it by experiment. While a constraint is active the core stops delivering absolute motion to that realm, keeps delivering relative_motion, freezes the position its own hit tests use, and - on a backend where it draws one - HIDES ITS OWN HUMAN CURSOR SPRITE. The app cannot hide that sprite and there is deliberately no message by which it could: the sprite is the core's, and a realm able to hide the human's pointer could mislead the human about where their input is going (vitrin_view states the same rule for the bitmap). The core therefore owns the un-hiding too, on every path that ends a constraint, without exception - a constraint that ended without its sprite returning would leave a human with no visible pointer, which is a worse failure than any this pair otherwise risks.
WHAT AN ACTIVE CONSTRAINT DOES NOT REACH. It never confines a principal's actuation: an emulated pointer move follows its grant and is delivered absolutely whatever this record says, so an app cannot acquire authority over an agent by locking a pointer. It never reaches the core's own overlays either - a consent card, the lock screen, the dead-man hold and the core's notice all take the pointer back, and each of those is a path on which this event reports the constraint inactive.

arg.name: serial
arg.summary: the serial of the pointer_constraint ask this concerns

arg.name: state
arg.summary: what the core did with that ask, and what is in force now

request.name: idle_inhibit

description.summary: ask the core not to blank this realm's screen while it is being watched

request.description:
The confined app's ask, relayed by its shim: "do not blank the screen while this plays". THE APP ASKS AND THE CORE DECIDES, the same direction pointer_constraint runs in and the opposite of request_selection - a reader who carries the clipboard's direction over to this message will read every rule below backwards.
THE SHIM AGGREGATES; THE WIRE CARRIES ONE BIT PER REALM. An app may hold any number of zwp_idle_inhibitor_v1 objects at once, and the core has no use for the count: it is deciding one question about one panel. So the shim sends held when its live-inhibitor count rises from zero and released when it falls back to zero, and nothing in between. That places the per-object bookkeeping on the side that can see object lifetimes and leaves the core holding a fact it can actually evaluate.
ONE MESSAGE IS THE WHOLE STATE, and released is the WITHDRAWAL - pointer_constraint's kind none discipline, for its reason: there is no separate unset message a withdrawal could race a set against, and no order in which the two could be applied wrongly. Repetition is legal and idempotent: a second held while held changes nothing, so a shim that resends after a reconnect or a surface change is correct rather than merely tolerated.
NO SERIAL AND NO VERDICT EVENT, and both absences are argued rather than left to look like omissions. A serial names the answer an ask expects, and this ask has none. There is no verdict because there is nowhere to deliver one: zwp_idle_inhibitor_v1 defines no events at all, so an app's only observable is whether its screen blanked, and a refusal is therefore unobservable AND harmless - a deployment that blanks nothing has satisfied the ask vacuously. That is why the razor's recoverable half has nothing to carry here, and it is the one place this pair differs from pointer_constraint, whose app IS waiting for an activation and would latch forever without one.
WHAT THE CORE HONOURS, stated on the wire because an app must not have to discover it by experiment: an inhibit holds off the blank only while the human's output is bound to the realm that holds it. An inhibit from a realm the human is not looking at holds nothing, and stops holding the moment they look elsewhere - no new ask, and no message saying so. A background realm able to pin the human's panel awake would be an ambient power-and-attention channel, which is what Wayland's own advice ("inhibitors should only be in effect while this surface is visible") says in the compositor's voice.
THAT GATE BOUNDS WAYLAND'S ADVICE AND DOES NOT DISCHARGE IT, stated plainly so no shim author reads the realm gate as more than it is. The gate asks whether the human is looking at this REALM, never whether this SURFACE is visible. A shim aggregates its app's inhibitor objects, and nothing here requires it to stop counting one whose surface has been unmapped but not destroyed - so an app holding a live inhibitor over a surface it has hidden still holds off the blank, for as long as the human is looking at that realm. That is per-realm gating's accepted cost, the same cost the surface paragraph below records, and it is a named gap rather than a defect in either side's implementation.
IT SUPPRESSES THE BLANK AND NEVER THE LOCK. The two are separate mechanisms that share one activity clock, and this message writes no clock: it adds a term to the blank's own decision and nothing else, so an idle lock still raises on time with an inhibit held. A comfort request from a confined app must not be able to disable a security control - and the consequence for the human is named rather than hidden: a film longer than the idle-lock timeout gets a lock screen over it, exactly as it would with no inhibit at all.
THE RECORD IS THE CORE'S, AND EXACTLY TWO PATHS DROP IT: this message carrying released, and the realm dying (the teardown funnel every death path reaches, so an app killed mid-film needs nobody to send anything). There are no others. The two absences are specified HERE rather than left for a shim author to find by experiment, because a shim author reads this document and nothing else.
A SEAT HANDOVER DOES NOT DROP IT, and this is the one place the message departs from pointer_constraint, which the core withdraws on a pause. The difference is RECOVERABILITY: a withdrawal is announced on the wire by pointer_constraint_state and the app may ask again, while this message has no verdict event, so a core-side drop would be silent AND permanent - the app's inhibitor object is still alive, its count never changes again, and no further held would ever follow. Nothing is decided by keeping the record: while the seat is away the core suppresses the blank countdown for the whole pause and holds the screen lit, so a retained inhibit changes no outcome.
THE HUMAN'S DEAD-MAN CHORD DOES NOT DROP IT EITHER, for that reason plus one: the chord destroys AUTHORITY, and an inhibit is not authority - no grant confers it and no revocation reaches it. The chord is also physical input, so pressing it stamps the activity clock and holds the screen lit whatever this record says. A human taking their session back therefore never has to get past an inhibit to see their own screen, which is why dropping the record would buy nothing and cost the app its only ask.
THE SHIM'S OWN RELEASE IS DRIVEN BY OBJECT DESTRUCTION rather than by app cooperation, so an app that exits without destroying its inhibitor still releases it. Two layers exist - that release and the realm's death - because a leaked inhibit that pins a human's panel awake forever is the worst failure this message can cause, and one layer of defence against it is a layer that can be forgotten.
surface MUST be null when state is released, and MUST name a surface this connection minted when it is held; the core ignores it in the released case rather than treating a decorated withdrawal as data. The core records which surface was named and gates per REALM today, not per surface - a named cost, carried for the reason pointer_constraint carries lifetime: a signature is immutable forever, nothing in this protocol hard-codes one surface per shim, and per-surface gating could not be added later without a whole new message.
A HELD CARRYING A NULL SURFACE violates that MUST, and the consequence is SPECIFIED rather than left open, because an unspecified consequence is the one thing two conformant implementations can disagree about while both believing they are right: the core RECORDS the ask with no surface named, that realm holds the blank exactly as any other held would, and NO error is raised. Null is legal wire for a nullable argument, and killing an app's shim over a missing decoration would answer a recoverable mistake fatally. A peer MAY log it; it MUST NOT answer it with invalid_object or invalid_argument.
ERRORS. What is fatal is unchanged decode-level ground: a surface id this connection never minted, or one at or below its watermark, is invalid_object (the shim violating its OWN object graph), and an out-of-range state is invalid_argument - on a shim connection both mean log-and-close. This request adds NO log-only condition of its own: an inhibit naming a surface that has never committed is a legitimate ask that simply holds nothing, not a bad_order.
NAME IT idle_inhibit, never bare "inhibit": Wayland has a second inhibitor (keyboard shortcuts) which this protocol does not serve, and an identifier that did not say which one it meant would be a collision waiting for the day it does - the same rule pointer_constraint states for the word "constraint".

enum.description:
Answers are exhaustive rather than optional: every request_selection gets exactly one selection, and a shim with nothing to give says so. The three refusing entries are distinguished because they mean different things to a human debugging a clipboard that did not work - "I selected nothing", "I selected a picture", and "I selected too much" are three different mistakes with three different fixes - and because the core journals which one it saw, with no content.
Entries are appended, never renumbered, like every enum here.

entry.summary: mime and data carry the app's selection

enum.name: pointer_constraint_kind

description.summary: what a pointer_constraint asks for, including nothing

enum.description:
The three things one ask can say. lock pins the pointer where it is and leaves relative_motion as the only movement the app receives; confine lets the pointer keep moving but keeps it inside the region. none WITHDRAWS whatever this connection had, and carrying it here is why there is no separate unset message to race.
Entries are appended, never renumbered, like every enum here.

entry.name: none
entry.summary: withdraw this connection's constraint; surface MUST be null

entry.name: lock
entry.summary: pin the pointer; movement reaches the app as relative_motion only

entry.name: confine
