enum.name: pointer_constraint_lifetime

description.summary: whether a constraint survives its own deactivation

enum.description:
Wayland's own two, carried across so a shim never has to invent a policy its app did not ask for. oneshot ends for good the first time it deactivates: the record is dropped and the app's object is finished with. persistent may deactivate and become active again with no new ask - which is what makes a realm switch survivable, since the human coming back re-activates what they left.
persistent survives a DEACTIVATION, not a WITHDRAWAL: a state of withdrawn is terminal for the serial that carries it, so a constraint the core withdrew - a seat pause, the dead-man chord - needs a new ask, and the app is told by the withdrawn rather than left to discover it.
Entries are appended, never renumbered, like every enum here.

entry.name: oneshot
entry.summary: ends for good at its first deactivation

entry.name: persistent
entry.summary: may deactivate and reactivate with no new ask

enum.name: pointer_constraint_status

description.summary: what the core did with a pointer_constraint, and what is in force

enum.description:
THE ZERO VALUE IS DELIBERATELY NOT AN "ok". That departs from selection_status, where ok is 0, and the departure is argued here rather than left standing as an inconsistency: zero is where a mis-decode and a zeroed struct both land, and "not constrained" is the safe reading of a byte nobody can trust, while "constrained" is not.
inactive and active are the two live states, and one record moves between them as often as the human's own actions require, with no further ask. withdrawn, refused and superseded are terminal for the serial that carries them: nothing follows on that serial ever again.
Entries are appended, never renumbered, like every enum here.

entry.name: inactive
entry.summary: recorded but not in force; may become active later with no new ask

entry.name: active
entry.summary: in force: absolute motion stops, relative_motion continues, the core hides its own cursor sprite

entry.name: withdrawn
entry.summary: the record is gone: the shim withdrew it, or what it named went away

entry.name: refused
entry.summary: not recorded at all; the app's object stays inert and this serial is not re-asked

entry.name: superseded
entry.summary: a later ask on this connection replaced it; this serial gets nothing further

enum.name: idle_inhibit_state

description.summary: whether a realm is holding an idle inhibit

enum.description:
Two entries, because the shim aggregates however many zwp_idle_inhibitor_v1 objects its app holds into one bit (see idle_inhibit). There is no count on the wire and there is deliberately no room for one: a count would make the core the bookkeeper of object lifetimes it cannot see.
THE ZERO VALUE IS "NOT INHIBITED", on pointer_constraint_status' rule and for its reason: zero is where a mis-decode and a zeroed struct both land, and the safe reading of a byte nobody can trust is that the human's screen may blank. "Hold this panel awake" must never be what a zero means.
Entries are appended, never renumbered, like every enum here.

entry.name: released
entry.summary: this realm holds no inhibit; surface MUST be null

entry.name: held
entry.summary: this realm asks that the screen not blank while its output is on the panel

interface.name: vitrin_shim_surface
interface.description: The buffer path from shim to core, with Wayland's proven pending-state semantics: attach and damage mutate pending state only; commit atomically latches it. Buffers are identified by shim-chosen cookies (buffer_id) rather than buffer objects; the buffer_done event echoes the cookie to return ownership. On connection death the core closes every fd it holds.

request.name: attach
request.description: Stages a buffer for the next commit. buffer_id is a shim-chosen cookie naming this buffer in later buffer_done events. In version-1 practice kind is shm: a memfd the core copies in at commit. kind dmabuf is the same message - single-plane, linear modifier implied (there is deliberately no modifier argument the core could fail to honor); explicit modifiers and multi-planar formats arrive as a since-gated parameter builder in a later version, one fd per message, so the one-fd rule never becomes a wall. Geometry inconsistent with the fd's actual size, a zero dimension, or a stride overflow is the log-and-close condition invalid_buffer; re-attaching a dmabuf buffer_id that has not yet received buffer_done is bad_order.

request.name: damage
request.description: Adds a buffer-coordinate damage rectangle to pending state. Repeatable; rectangles accumulate as a union until commit and travel per-rectangle on the wire so damage-only updates are verifiable in logs. Damage is a hint - the core may repaint more - and out-of-bounds rectangles are clamped, not fatal.

request.name: commit
request.description: Latches pending attach and damage atomically into the surface's current state. A commit with no new attach re-presents the current buffer with the new damage (a repaint) - legal, not an error. Damage or commit against a surface that has never been attached is the log-and-close condition bad_order.

event.name: frame_done
event.description: The frame-callback relay: sent after a commit's content has been presented (or would have been, headless). At most one outstanding frame_done per commit, FIFO-correlated; the shim fans it out to its app's frame callbacks so the app throttles to the true output cadence. frame_done is per commit and independent of buffer disposition: a commit whose attached buffer failed (buffer_done with a failure status) re-presents the previous content and still receives its frame_done, so the app's pacing loop never stalls on a rejected buffer.

arg.name: time_ms
arg.summary: presentation time in milliseconds, monotonic domain

event.name: buffer_done

description.summary: buffer ownership returns (exactly once per attach)

event.description:
Terminal disposition of one attach, exactly once per attach, in attach order per surface - including an attach superseded by another attach before commit, which is released promptly without being used. Status released means the core (and GPU) are done with the buffer: the shim, and its app, may reuse it - prompt after the copy under version-1 shm copy-in, at GPU-done under dmabuf passthrough (the same message; only the timing regime changes). The failure statuses mean the buffer was not used (the previously committed content remains on screen) and direct the shim to fall back to shm; ownership returns in the same breath. Deliberately not merged with frame_done: buffer reusability and frame pacing are different facts that only coincide under copy-in.
File-descriptor ownership: the core takes ownership of the fd received in attach and closes it before or as it emits this event for that buffer_id (after copying the pixels out under shm, or after importing under dmabuf, or immediately on a failure status). The shim owns its buffer, never the passed fd, once buffer_done arrives. On connection death the core closes every attach fd it still holds.

entry.name: shm
entry.summary: memfd; the core copies pixels in at commit

entry.name: dmabuf
entry.summary: dmabuf; the core imports it zero-copy, single-plane, linear modifier implied

entry.name: released
entry.summary: the buffer was used (or superseded) and may be reused

entry.name: import_failed
entry.summary: dmabuf import failed; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

entry.name: format_unsupported
entry.summary: format not usable by the renderer; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

entry.name: too_large
entry.summary: buffer exceeds the renderer's limits; fall back to shm; buffer unused and released

interface.name: vitrin_shim_seat

description.summary: input delivery to the shim (events only, origin-tagged)

interface.description:
Input delivery from core to shim. The shim replays these events to its app through its own virtual seat; the core owns the mapping from principals to shim seats. Every event carries origin as its final argument - per-event tagging, never modal start/stop envelopes (modal state desyncs and fuzzes badly) - preserving the physical-versus-emulated distinction end to end from day one, because physically-originated consent in a later phase is built on it. This structural rule is enforced by the schema.
Pointer coordinates are realm-view pixels; the shim maps view to surface-local coordinates. Focus in version 1 is synthesized shim-side (a single-surface realm: pointer enter on first motion, keyboard focus held on the app); an explicit tagged focus event is the multi-surface addition of a later version.
Version 1 delivers ONE shared pointer position per realm view: these events carry origin, not principal identity, so a realm's app sees a single pointer whoever moved it. That is the version-1 half of the per-principal cursor model (see vitrin_actuator_pointer), and the reason the core needs a defensive rule keeping emulated motion from relocating the position a consent grab hit-tests. Per-principal delivery arrives as since-gated sibling events that also name the principal, each still ending with origin so the B2 rule holds; the version-1 five stay valid forever, and so does everything appended to them.
VERSION 2 APPENDS FIVE MORE, and appending is the only way this interface ever grows: relative_motion, and the four that carry a touchpad gesture - gesture_begin, gesture_swipe_update, gesture_pinch_update, gesture_end. They exist because a pointer vocabulary of destinations alone cannot express what a pointer lock delivers or what two fingers do, not because a device set demanded arguments of its own: every argument in the five is a delta, a finger count, a scale, a rotation or a tag, and none of them names a device. Touch and tablet have no event here, and they are NOT YET SERVED rather than refused - a difference that is load-bearing. What kept them out is a measurement of one machine's devices, which is evidence about a machine and not a property of a class, and a permanent wire protocol may not foreclose a device class on that ground. What would reopen each is recorded in this repository's decision log rather than here, because a wire can say what it carries but cannot say what evidence would change it.

event.name: motion
event.description: Pointer motion to realm-view (x, y). Coordinates are fixed-point so that later server-side motion synthesis can be sub-pixel without a signature change (the agent-facing move request stays integer because agents address captured pixels).

event.name: button
event.description: Button press or release at the current pointer position; Linux evdev button codes.

event.name: scroll
event.description: High-resolution scroll; one wheel notch is plus or minus 120.

event.name: key
event.description:
A key event for the human path: physical typing flows core to shim to app, and humans press chords, arrows, and function keys that a text string cannot carry. Keys travel as xkbcommon keysyms, not keycodes: layout-independent, requiring no keymap-relay message, and the shim maps keysyms into the same dynamically generated keymap machinery that text delivery already requires.
Where the keysym is resolved is a property of the core's backend and not of this wire. A nested core receives keys the host compositor has already interpreted and interprets nothing itself. A core driving physical input devices directly receives evdev scancodes and nothing else, so it resolves them against a keymap of its own before sending this event. Both produce a modifier-resolved keysym, both leave the wire and this interface unchanged, and a shim cannot tell them apart - which is the point, and is why the earlier claim that no keymap interpretation happens inside the core was corrected rather than made normative.
Normative modifier-suppression rule: keysyms arrive already modifier-resolved. The shim MUST bind each non-modifier keysym at an unmodified (plain) level of its dynamic keymap for replay, so that modifiers already applied are never applied twice. Modifier keysyms (Shift_L, Control_L, Alt_L, Super_L, and friends) are forwarded as ordinary key events and convey chord state to the app only; they MUST NOT change the level at which subsequent resolved keysyms bind. Documented version-1 limitation: raw-scancode fidelity for keymap-sensitive apps is a later version's keymap relay plus keycode event.

event.name: text
event.description: Text delivery - the agent actuation path in version 1, always origin emulated. The shim renders the string via its dynamic keymap; a newline MUST be rendered as Return and a tab as Tab, mirroring the actuator contract. The origin tag on text is what keeps a later phase's human input-method text (origin physical) purely additive.

event.name: relative_motion
event.description:
Pointer motion expressed as a delta rather than as a destination. This event ACCOMPANIES motion, it does not replace it: one physical movement produces both, and a shim replays both, because an app binds whichever of the two it understands and must not be made to guess which one this core sends. Deltas are realm-view pixels and are fixed-point for motion's reason.
TWO DELTAS, NOT ONE, and both are load-bearing. dx and dy are the movement after the core applied pointer acceleration - the movement that agrees with where the pointer visibly went. dx_unaccel and dy_unaccel are the same movement before acceleration, which is what a camera control or a drawing tool wants and is most of the reason this event exists at all. Carrying one alone would force a shim to copy it into the other, producing a field it would then be lying about; carrying both leaves the choice with the app that knows which it needs.
NO TIMESTAMP, deliberately. No event on this interface carries one, and a shim stamps each replay with its own clock. A device clock on the wire beside that one is a second, unsynchronised clock, which this system refuses elsewhere for the same reason. The cost is real and is paid rather than argued away: a consumer integrating deltas over dt gets the time the shim replayed them, not the time the device produced them.
NO PAIRING OF ITS OWN - there is no begin and no end. Where a latch could form is the pointer lock this event is the input half of: a lock stops absolute motion and freezes the position the core's own hit tests use, so a lock whose end is lost is a pointer that never moves again. That is why such state is the core's to own and to end, on every path that takes input away, and why an emulated motion must not relocate the frozen position - the defensive rule this interface's description already asks for, now with a second reason to want it.
THE LOCK ITSELF IS NOT AN EVENT ON THIS INTERFACE, and the reason is structural. Every event here ends with origin, and origin has exactly two values: a human's device, or a principal's actuator. A lock is asked for by the confined app, which is neither, so any tag it carried would be false - on the one interface whose whole design idea is that the tag never drifts. The ask and the core's verdict therefore belong on vitrin_shim_session, which already carries shim-to-core requests, and version 2 defines them there: the pointer_constraint request and the pointer_constraint_state event. This event is emitted for ordinary unlocked motion as well as under a lock - it is the input half either way, and a lock changes what accompanies it rather than whether it arrives. Name it "pointer lock" or "pointer constraint" and never bare "constraint": in this protocol that word already means a PETITION constraint (vitrin_realm.request_grant's flags - request_grant is a request on the realm handle, not on vitrin_grant).
Version 2 defines no emulated source of a delta - the agent-facing vitrin_actuator_pointer.move is absolute - so a version-2 core emits this event with origin physical only. The tag is mandatory here as everywhere on this interface, and is exactly what keeps a later emulated source purely additive.

event.name: gesture_begin
event.description:
A multi-finger touchpad gesture began. Swipe and pinch SHARE this event, and share gesture_end, because the begin and end signatures of the two are identical in the pointer-gesture vocabulary these events serve. A signature is immutable forever, so four events with no dead argument is the shape - rather than six with duplicated ones, and rather than two phase-tagged events whose deltas and completion flag would each be meaningless in two phases out of three. kind says which gesture began.
fingers is how many fingers the gesture began with, and is FIXED for its life: a gesture that gains or loses a finger ends, and a new one begins.
AT MOST ONE GESTURE IS IN FLIGHT PER SEAT. Every gesture_swipe_update, gesture_pinch_update and gesture_end that follows belongs to this begin until that end. The core does not send a second begin while one is in flight, and does not send an update or an end for a begin it did not send. A shim that receives one anyway has met a core bug and IGNORES it: it must not replay a gesture its app never saw begin, and it must not close the connection either, because an app must not die of the core's mistake. Log-and-close on a shim connection is for a SHIM's own violations; this is not one.
WHAT THE CORE OWES IN RETURN is exactly one gesture_end for every gesture_begin it sent, without exception. A begin with no end leaves an app accumulating a gesture forever, which is the latched-modifier failure wearing a new shape. When something takes input away mid-gesture for good - a realm switch, a seat pause - the core MINTS an end, cancelled, rather than dropping the gesture silently. gesture_end states which paths those are, and which paths withhold a gesture's updates without minting one.
In version 2 the only source is a physical device: no actuator mints a gesture and no verb grants one. The origin tag is mandatory anyway, and is what keeps a later emulated source a pure addition rather than a change here.

arg.name: fingers
arg.summary: finger count, fixed for this gesture's life

event.name: gesture_swipe_update
event.description:
How far the finger group moved since the previous event of the gesture in flight, in realm-view pixels. A DELTA, never a position, and never cumulative.
Valid only between a gesture_begin whose kind is swipe and that gesture's gesture_end. It is a separate event from gesture_pinch_update rather than a shared one, because pinch additionally carries scale and rotation: a single shared update would freeze two arguments meaningless for swipe into a signature that can never afterwards be changed.

arg.name: dx
arg.summary: delta x since this gesture's previous event, realm-view pixels

arg.name: dy
arg.summary: delta y since this gesture's previous event, realm-view pixels

event.name: gesture_pinch_update

description.summary: an in-flight pinch moved, scaled or rotated

event.description:
The motion of the pinch in flight. Valid only between a gesture_begin whose kind is pinch and that gesture's gesture_end.
THE FOUR QUANTITIES DO NOT SHARE A REFERENCE POINT, and reading one as though it were another is the mistake this paragraph exists to prevent.
dx and dy are how far the centre of the finger group moved since THIS GESTURE'S PREVIOUS EVENT, in realm-view pixels. Deltas.
scale is the pinch's scale relative to ITS OWN BEGIN, not to the previous event. It is 1.0 at the begin, and an app applies it to the size the object had at the begin - multiplying successive values into a running product is wrong and compounds. Absolute, not a delta.
rotation is the angle turned since THIS GESTURE'S PREVIOUS EVENT, in degrees, positive clockwise. A delta again.
That asymmetry is inherited rather than invented: it is what the pointer-gesture vocabulary defines and what the device layer under the core reports. It is written out here because a wire that quietly reinterpreted either quantity would be wrong in a way apps cannot detect - a scale read as a delta zooms toward zero, and a rotation read as absolute snaps back on every event.

arg.name: dx
arg.summary: centre delta x since this gesture's previous event, realm-view pixels

arg.name: dy
arg.summary: centre delta y since this gesture's previous event, realm-view pixels

arg.name: scale
arg.summary: scale relative to this gesture's begin, 1.0 at the begin

arg.name: rotation
arg.summary: degrees turned since this gesture's previous event, positive clockwise

event.name: gesture_end
event.description:
Ends the gesture the last gesture_begin started. This is the second half of the guarantee gesture_begin states: exactly one of these per begin the core sent, always, on every path.
state distinguishes the two ways a gesture stops, and the distinction is what lets an app commit rather than guess. completed means the human finished it and what it did should stand. cancelled means it did not finish and a preview should be undone. Cancelled covers the device layer's own cancellation AND the core's own. Version 2 ends a gesture cancelled on exactly two core paths: a realm switch, and a seat pause. On both, the human's fingers are still down and no end can ever arrive, so an end is minted rather than waited for. A consent prompt and a screen lock do NOT mint one: they withhold the gesture's updates and then deliver the device's own end when the human lifts, so no latch forms - but an app that was previewing is told the human completed what they in fact abandoned. That gap is named here rather than smoothed over, and closing it is owed. Where an end IS minted, the app is told the truth about the gesture rather than a convenient falsehood about the human, which is the same trade this system already makes for keys and buttons held across such a moment.
kind repeats the in-flight gesture's kind. It is redundant by construction - only one gesture is ever in flight - and it is carried anyway so that a disagreement with what the shim has in flight is a DETECTABLE core bug rather than a silent mis-replay. A shim that sees one ends the gesture it actually has and logs; as with an unpaired update, it does not close the connection over the core's mistake.

arg.name: kind
arg.summary: which gesture ended; repeats the in-flight kind

arg.name: state
arg.summary: whether the human completed the gesture

entry.name: released
entry.summary: key released

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: key pressed

enum.name: origin
enum.description: The libei/EIS distinction, preserved through the hop where libei drops it: physical means a real human input device produced this event; emulated means a principal's actuator (or, later, motion synthesis) produced it. Present on every seat event as the final argument, from day one, because later phases hang physically-originated consent on it.

entry.name: physical
entry.summary: produced by a physical human input device

entry.name: emulated
entry.summary: produced by a principal's actuator

enum.name: gesture_kind

description.summary: which gesture a shared begin or end names

enum.description:
gesture_begin and gesture_end are shared by every gesture kind, so this is the argument that says which one. Version 2 defines two: swipe, whose motion arrives as gesture_swipe_update, and pinch, whose motion arrives as gesture_pinch_update.
A FURTHER KIND IS AN APPENDED ENTRY, not a new begin or end. A hold, for instance, has the same begin and end shape and no motion at all, so serving it would add one entry here and no event - which is the whole reason begin and end are shared. Values are immutable and entries are never renumbered, like every enum here. Nothing beyond swipe and pinch is served yet; that is not-yet, and what would reopen it is recorded in this repository's decision log rather than on the wire.

entry.name: swipe
entry.summary: multi-finger swipe; motion arrives as gesture_swipe_update

entry.name: pinch
entry.summary: pinch; motion arrives as gesture_pinch_update

enum.name: gesture_state
enum.description: The two ways gesture_end can arrive. This is an enum rather than a bare flag because every state argument on this interface is enum-typed and because the difference is what an app acts on: a completed pinch keeps its zoom, a cancelled one puts it back.

entry.name: completed
entry.summary: the human finished the gesture

entry.name: cancelled
entry.summary: the gesture did not finish; a preview should be undone

interface.name: vitrin_launcher
interface.description:
The launch capability: start the app a realm template names, into a fresh realm instance. Minted by vitrin_grant.get_launcher and born inert - it confers nothing until its grant resolves granted with realm_launch in the effective verb set, every launch passes the single enforcement chokepoint, and a refused launch is recoverable through vitrin_grant.refused, never fatal.
THE COMMAND NEVER CROSSES THE WIRE. launch takes no arguments. The realm this grant was petitioned over names a realm TEMPLATE, and the template names the program. Whoever may write a deployment's realm configuration is who chooses what the trusted core spawns; a command string off the wire would hand that choice to any principal holding one grant and would leave the audit of that configuration with nothing to audit. This is the same reason vitrin_realm carries no launch request: naming is not authority, so holding a realm handle must never confer the power to start a process. Selecting WHICH program to run is therefore done by petitioning over a different realm, at consent time, in front of the human - never by an argument after the fact.
WHAT THIS FACET IS NOT. It cannot stop, restart or reconfigure a realm, and there is deliberately no request that does: this interface's whole authority is "create one more realm from a template the operator wrote". Lifecycle beyond creation is not expressible here at any verb set.
WHAT A LAUNCH GRANT DOES NOT BOUND. A launched app is confined by whatever the deployment confines realms with, which this facet neither states nor strengthens. Authority to launch is authority to start a process under the core's own uid and filesystem view unless something outside this protocol says otherwise; the grant bounds WHO may launch and HOW OFTEN, never what the launched program may then do.
Version 1 does not define this interface's messages at all - it is reachable only through a since="2" mint. The realm_launch bit was defined before it was served, and the reference core has served it since WS-E.1.1 - a chokepoint arm and prompt copy of its own - so whether a petition for it is refused "unsupported" is a property of the deployment rather than of the wire: a deployment that will not host process creation answers "unsupported" rather than killing the connection. observe_cursor and egress are the TWO bits left in that defined-but-unserved posture, refused by every deployment - the first because per-principal cursor delivery does not exist, the second because the out-of-core proxy a connection would be made through does not exist. egress's reason narrowed when vitrin_egress landed and did not go away: a facet is a request to ask through, not a mechanism to answer with. Defining a verb before serving it is what makes a petition for it an answer rather than a connection death.

request.name: launch

description.summary: launch the granted template into a new realm

request.description:
Reply-bearing: exactly one terminal event per request - launched on success, or vitrin_grant.refused(realm_launch, ...) on failure - in request order, never coalesced. Pipelining launches is legal and replies pair in order, exactly as capture_frame's do. Launches are rate-limited by the grant's max_event_rate like every other use.
The request deliberately carries no arguments, and that is the security property rather than an economy: see THE COMMAND NEVER CROSSES THE WIRE above. A future need to parameterize a launch arrives as a since-gated sibling request or a builder preceding this one, never as arguments added here - this signature is frozen forever like every other.
EVERY LAUNCH CREATES A NEW REALM; NOTHING IS EVER RELAUNCHED. An exited realm stays exited, because "unavailable" must keep meaning not-ever: an agent that hears it stops asking, and reviving a realm behind that answer would make it a lie and would park consent prompts in front of humans about authority over a corpse. A template is therefore addressable but never itself paints: a grant to observe a template refuses no_surface forever, which is authority over nothing rather than authority over something dangerous.
Refusals a launch can receive are the grant-lifecycle ones (not_granted, expired, revoked, rate_limited), capacity when the deployment is at its realm limit, and internal for a spawn failure the core did not choose. It is never refused no_surface - a realm with no surface is what launch exists to fix - and never preempted or consent_held, which are attention-shaped and so reach actuation and the layout verbs rather than a launch.

event.name: launched
event.description:
Exactly one per successful launch, in request order, never coalesced. realm is the id of the newly created realm instance, immediately usable as vitrin_principal.get_realm's name - so an agent that launched an app petitions over the result exactly as it would over any other realm, with no shortcut and no implied authority. Launching confers NOTHING over what it launched: observing or actuating the new realm is a separate petition, seen by the human separately.
The id is minted by the core and is unique for the life of the session; it obeys the same realm-id rule every other realm id does, which is what lets it travel through get_realm unchanged. Its internal shape is the core's business and not something a client may parse or predict - treat it as opaque.

arg.name: realm
arg.summary: id of the newly created realm instance, usable as get_realm's name (max 64 bytes)

interface.name: vitrin_layout_focus
interface.description:
The focus capability: make the granted realm the one the output shows and the one input reaches. Minted by vitrin_grant.get_layout_focus and born inert - it confers nothing until its grant resolves granted with layout_focus in the effective verb set, every use passes the single enforcement chokepoint, and a refused use is recoverable through vitrin_grant.refused, never fatal.
FOCUS IS ONE ACT, NOT TWO. Showing a realm and directing the HUMAN'S OWN physical input to it are the same request here, and there is no verb set, and no attenuation, that separates them. A holder that could bind the output to realm A while the human's keystrokes continued to reach realm B - or the reverse - would be able to make a human type into a realm they cannot see, which is the sharpest form of the focus theft this verb is separated from layout_arrange in order to make attenuable. That coupling is an ordering rule, so it sits with the other four in SCENE AUTHORITY: no grant purchases it away.
This is a rule about PHYSICAL input, not about actuation. An agent's injected pointer and text are addressed to the realm its own grant names, are consented per realm and carry the emulated origin tag, so they are not the human's attention and are not governed by the binding.
WHAT THIS FACET IS NOT. It cannot raise, stack, place, resize or close anything, and there is deliberately no request that does. Neither can it read anything: which realm currently holds the output is not reported here or anywhere else on the wire, so a holder learns the effect of its own focus request only through a capture it holds separate authority for. Focus is a write, not a window into the session.
WHAT A FOCUS GRANT DOES NOT BOUND. The human's own input is not mediated by this grant and never yields to it: physical input in progress preempts a focus request exactly as it preempts an actuation, and the human's revocation gesture is unreachable from here.

request.name: focus

description.summary: bind the output to the granted realm and direct input there

request.description:
Fire-and-forget: no terminal event, and refusals may be coalesced per the delivery classification. The request deliberately carries NO ARGUMENTS - the realm this grant was petitioned over is the realm it focuses, so a holder can only ever focus what the human saw named on the consent prompt. A realm argument would let one grant move the output to a realm nobody consented to, which is the authority-over-a-name mistake vitrin_realm refuses in the same words.
Focusing the realm that is already focused is legal and is a no-op.
Focus is rate-limited by the grant's max_event_rate like every other use, which is what stops a holder from flickering the output between realms faster than a human can read it.
Refusals this request can receive are the grant-lifecycle ones (not_granted, expired, revoked, rate_limited), no_surface when the granted realm has no live view to show, the two attention-shaped ones an actuation can receive - preempted while physical human input owns the target, and consent_held while this principal's own consent prompt is up - and internal, for a server-side failure while carrying the focus out, on the same terms every other verb can meet it (vitrin_launcher.launch names it for the same reason). It is never refused capacity, which concerns creating a realm.
preempted here is CONDITIONAL: a server that defines the attention signal (vitrin_principal.attention, since version 2) does not refuse preempted while that signal is live for this principal. See vitrin_grant.refusal.
NOT REPLY-BEARING, deliberately. A terminal event would carry no information a subsequent capture does not already carry, and adding one would make the reply the place a client learns which realm is focused - a read this interface does not offer.

interface.name: vitrin_layout_arrange
interface.description:
The arrangement capability: choose whether the granted realm's view fills the output or is composited at the size its own app chose. Minted by vitrin_grant.get_layout_arrange and born inert on exactly the terms vitrin_layout_focus is.
ONE REQUEST, AND THE ABSENCES ARE THE DESIGN. There is no place, no resize, no raise, no lower, no close and no stacking request on this interface - not a request that refuses, but no request at all. The scene shows one realm at a time, unstacked and unoverlapped, at one output size; a place or raise request would have to either widen that scene or accept an argument it then ignored, and a verb that silently does less than its name is worse than one that has no request. Every one of those absences is therefore a statement about what a granted layout_arrange can and cannot do, and a deployment that adds a request here before its scene can honour it breaks the rule that a deployment MUST NOT grant a verb it does not enforce.
Growth arrives as since-gated sibling requests when the scene can honour them, exactly as every other interface grows, and never by changing set_fullscreen's meaning.
AT MOST ONE HOLDER PER OUTPUT. A petition for layout_arrange while the verb is already spoken for resolves "layout_held" at admission - it never reaches a human. Spoken for means either a live grant carrying the verb or ANOTHER PETITION STILL PENDING for it, and the pending half is deliberate: two petitions admitted while both waited could be approved by a human twice over and mint two holders, which is precisely the state this rule exists to make unreachable. So a petition that has not resolved yet really does hold the slot, and it frees it by resolving to anything other than granted. Arbitrating between two would-be arrangers is window-management policy, so the core refuses to arbitrate rather than choosing a rule. layout_focus carries no such restriction: focus is a momentary act rather than a standing arrangement, and several principals may hold it at once.
WHAT THIS FACET CANNOT REACH. The consent surface and the trust indicator are not part of any realm's view and no arrangement moves, resizes, occludes or fullscreens over them. That is an ordering invariant (see SCENE AUTHORITY), so it is not a check this interface performs on the way past - there is no request through which the attempt is even expressible.

request.name: set_fullscreen

description.summary: fill the output, or compose at the app's own size

request.description:
Fire-and-forget: no terminal event, and refusals may be coalesced per the delivery classification. Carries no realm argument for the same reason focus does not - the grant names the realm.
WHAT THE TWO MODES MEAN, precisely, because the difference is a size and not a decoration. FULLSCREEN means the realm's view size tracks the output's: the core sends vitrin_shim_session.configure with the output's size on entering the mode and again whenever the output resizes while the realm is in it, so the app fills the output edge to edge. WINDOWED means it does not: the core imposes no size at all, sends nothing, the realm's view keeps whatever size it already had, and the compositor letterboxes that buffer centered and unscaled inside the output. Re-sending configure is a documented permission of that event, not a new mechanism.
THE CORE NEVER INVENTS A WINDOW SIZE, and that is why "windowed" is an absence rather than a second size. A core that chose one would be choosing where a window goes and how big it is, which is window-management policy and belongs outside the core. The only two sizes in the system are the output's and the one the realm already has, and these two modes are exactly the choice between them.
A CONSEQUENCE WORTH STATING PLAINLY: while the output's size and the realm's size are equal, the two modes are indistinguishable and switching between them changes nothing an observer can see. They diverge the moment the output resizes under a windowed realm, and converge again the moment that realm is fullscreened. A client must not read a mode change as a guarantee that anything moved.
Setting the mode a realm is already in is legal and is a no-op.
This request is defined for the granted realm whether or not that realm holds the output. A realm arranged while hidden takes the arrangement with it when it is next focused; nothing here reads or changes the binding, which is layout_focus's alone.
Refusals are exactly vitrin_layout_focus.focus's set, for the same reasons: the grant-lifecycle codes, no_surface when the realm has no live view (an app that has committed nothing has no own size to return to, and no view to fill the output with), preempted or consent_held on the attention-shaped terms an actuation meets them, and internal for a server-side failure while carrying the arrangement out. preempted is CONDITIONAL on the same terms focus's is - the attention signal lifts it for both layout verbs or for neither, because "fullscreen on<Enter>" hits the identical loop that "focus editor<Enter>" does.

enum.name: mode

description.summary: the two arrangements this scene can express

enum.description: A closed pair rather than a boolean, so that a scene able to express a third arrangement appends an entry here instead of needing a second request. Values are immutable and entries append, like every other enum; an out-of-range value is fatal "invalid_argument".

entry.name: windowed
entry.summary: compose the realm's view at the size its own app last committed, letterboxed centered and unscaled inside the output

entry.name: fullscreen
entry.summary: configure the realm's view to the output's size, so the app fills the output

interface.name: vitrin_egress
interface.description:
The outbound-reach capability: open one connection to the single host:port the granted resource selector names, and hand the connected socket to the principal as a file descriptor. Minted by vitrin_grant.get_egress and born inert - it confers nothing until its grant resolves granted with egress in the effective verb set, every connection passes the single enforcement chokepoint, and a refused connection is recoverable, never fatal.
NOTHING SERVES THIS INTERFACE, AT ANY DEPLOYMENT, TODAY. egress is refused "unsupported" by every deployment (vitrin_grant.verb), so no grant can resolve granted carrying it, so every request_connect through every facet minted from every grant refuses "not_granted". What is missing is the out-of-core mediating proxy the connection would be made through; this interface is the request to ask through, which is a different thing from a mechanism to answer with. It is defined ahead of that mechanism for the reason every staged verb in this document is: a client asking for authority nobody serves must get an answer rather than a dead socket, and a facet that refuses on first use leaks nothing about why.
THE REFERENCE CORE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT THESE MESSAGES AT ALL, which is a stronger statement than the paragraph above and is stated separately so it is not read as the same one. vitrind's dispatch has no arm for get_egress or for request_connect: sending either today is answered "invalid_opcode" and the connection dies, where this document says the mint is always legal and the use refuses recoverably. That is a gap between this document and the shipped binary, owned by the task that lands the proxy, and it is written here because a reader of the IDL has no other way to learn it.
A SEPARATE INTERFACE FROM THE FILESYSTEM POWERBOX, and the dialect decides that rather than taste. interface/@verb is one value per interface, so an interface declaring verb="designate_file" cannot also declare verb="egress"; its egress requests would reach the enforcement chokepoint with no verb to check them against. That is the same rule that made the layout facet TWO interfaces (vitrin_layout_focus and vitrin_layout_arrange), and it produces the same answer here: the powerbox carries the file half, this interface carries the socket half, and "the socket analog of request_file" survives as the SHAPE of the request rather than as a claim about which interface hosts it.
WHAT THIS FACET IS NOT. It cannot listen, cannot bind, cannot name a second endpoint, and cannot resolve a name on the principal's behalf. There is deliberately no request that does any of those: a realm's network namespace holds exactly lo and nothing routable, so inbound reach is not a thing this protocol can attenuate - it is a thing the realm does not have. Adding a listen request would be adding the authority, not exposing it.
WHAT AN EGRESS GRANT DOES NOT BOUND, and this is the residue worth knowing before petitioning for one. The delivered fd is kernel authority, and revoking the grant does not reach into the realm and close it. What revocation does reach is the far end: the socket is a connection made BY the proxy, so the proxy holds the other side and can close it, which is why live connections are torn down on revocation where a delivered FILE descriptor's contents are not recallable at all. That difference is real and is stated rather than generalized from the powerbox's residue - but nothing implements either half today, so it describes what the design is built to and not what any deployment does.
Version 1 does not define this interface's messages at all - it is reachable only through a since="2" mint. The egress bit is NOT version-gated: a version-1 connection may name it in a petition and is answered "unsupported", because a bitfield is one mask checked identically on every negotiated version.

request.name: request_connect

description.summary: open one outbound connection to a granted endpoint

request.description:
Reply-bearing: exactly ONE terminal event per request, in request order, never coalesced. Unlike a fire-and-forget actuation, whose refusals may be coalesced, this request's answer is a resource the client is waiting for, so its terminals pair one-to-one exactly as capture_frame's and launch's do.
THREE TERMINALS, NOT TWO, and that is this interface's one departure from every other reply-bearing request in this document. Stated first because a client must handle all three:
- connected(fd, host, port) - the chokepoint admitted the use and the connection was made; - vitrin_grant.refused(egress, code, ...) - the chokepoint withheld the authority, or this server failed while carrying the use out; - connect_failed(reason) - the chokepoint ADMITTED the use and the far end did not answer.
WHY THE THIRD EXISTS. vitrin_grant.refused is the enforcement chokepoint's voice: every code in its enum is something a server DECIDED about a grant. A host that is down decided nothing about any grant, and there is no honest code for it. not_granted would be the worst available lie, because an agent that hears it correctly stops asking - which is right for a withheld authority and wrong for a host that is briefly unreachable. internal names a failure of THIS server (renderer, memfd, delivery), and the far end is not this server. no_surface is about the realm's own window. Rounding a transport failure into any of them would make "refused" stop meaning "authority was withheld", which is the one thing it has to keep meaning.
Keeping the two apart is not an ergonomic nicety in a capability system, it is the distinction between "you may not" and "it did not work", and blurring it is a bug in both directions: an agent that reads a transport failure as a lost authority abandons work it is permitted to do, and an agent that reads a refusal as a transient failure retries forever against a wall. The cost is named rather than hidden: clients now have three terminals to handle here and AT MOST TWO anywhere else - two on capture_frame and launch, one apiece on sync and request_grant - and the asymmetry is bought deliberately. What does NOT move is the rule itself: every reply-bearing request still receives exactly one terminal. Three is the size of the set this request's one terminal is drawn from, not a number of events it receives.
AUTHORITY IS DECIDED BEFORE ANYTHING TOUCHES THE NETWORK, and the order is normative rather than an implementation preference. The chokepoint answers first; only an admitted use reaches the proxy. So connect_failed is unreachable for a principal whose grant does not cover the endpoint, and no probe of this interface can measure the reachability of a host the asker was not authorized to reach. A principal that IS authorized does learn whether that one endpoint answers - which is inside what the grant approved, since the authority to reach an endpoint is the authority to discover that it is down - and that is named here rather than left to be found.
WHY THIS REQUEST NAMES AN ENDPOINT AT ALL, when the grant already names one. Today the net: grammar admits exactly one host and one port, so a facet minted from a grant addresses exactly one endpoint and these arguments look redundant. They are not redundant by design, and a signature is frozen forever, so the room has to be here now or never: request_grant's resource vocabulary grows by version without a new request, and the ergonomics answer this design has already committed to for browser-shaped realms is an enumerated template - a named, fully enumerated host:port set the human approves as an enumeration. A grant over such a resource covers more than one endpoint, and the request has to say which one it wants.
NAMING AN ENDPOINT IS NOT AUTHORITY OVER IT. The chokepoint compares what this request names against what the grant covers, and the comparison can only ever narrow: an endpoint outside the grant refuses "not_granted", and every endpoint inside it was on the consent card. That is vitrin_realm's naming-is-not-authority rule applied at use time. It is also the exact contrast with vitrin_launcher.launch, which takes NO arguments because there the empty signature is the security property - a command chosen after consent would be a program the human never saw. Here the endpoint crosses the wire and chooses nothing.
host is the host half of the grant's net: selector spelled EXACTLY as that selector spells it, with one difference stated so it is not guessed: an IPv6 literal is carried WITHOUT its brackets. The brackets exist only to keep the selector's final colon unambiguous, and this request carries the port as its own argument, so there is nothing to disambiguate and admitting brackets would give one endpoint two spellings under one selector. Comparison is byte-exact, on the same terms and for the same reasons the selector's is: Example.com and example.com are two strings, a grant naming one does not cover the other, and erring narrow is the only direction this comparison may be wrong in.
The 253-byte bound is the DNS name maximum, stated in its own terms rather than derived from resource's 256-byte bound. It is the LOOSER of the two: a host of 251 bytes fits here and fits in no net: selector, so it is accepted by the decoder and refused "not_granted" by the chokepoint, which is the fail-closed direction.
THE FATAL-VS-RECOVERABLE RAZOR FOR THIS REQUEST. Fatal, all of them grammar: a malformed frame; this opcode on a version-1 connection ("invalid_opcode"); a host longer than its bound; a port outside 1-65535 ("invalid_argument"). The port rule is argument validation the decoder cannot do, exactly like request_grant's non-zero-verbs rule, and it is FATAL where the same mistake inside a net: selector resolves "unsupported" - the two differ because a selector is a string whose only wire constraint is a byte length and whose content is a policy question, while port here is a numeric argument with a stated domain, the same shape as an enum. Everything else is recoverable: every authority answer, every server-side failure, and every transport outcome, including the case where the deployment serves no egress at all.

arg.name: host
arg.summary: the host half of the grant's net: selector, byte-exact, IPv6 literals WITHOUT brackets (max 253 bytes)

arg.name: port
arg.summary: the port half of the grant's net: selector; outside 1-65535 is fatal invalid_argument

event.name: connected

description.summary: the connected socket for one admitted request_connect

event.description:
Exactly one per successful request_connect, in request order, never coalesced. fd is a connected stream socket to the endpoint named, already open; the principal owns it and closes it.
ONE FD PER MESSAGE, which is the wire's rule and not this interface's choice: a message carries at most one file descriptor, so a request that needed two sockets would be two requests. A client receiving this event with no fd, or with more than one, has met a transport violation and treats it as fatal - the same rule frame_ready is delivered under.
host and port ECHO what the server connected to, and the echo is not decoration. Replies pair in request order, which is a bookkeeping obligation on the client; if that bookkeeping is wrong, a mis-paired frame shows the wrong pixels and a mis-paired SOCKET sends whatever the agent writes next to the wrong host. The echo turns an assumption into something the client can check, which is the same reason sync's cookie is echoed by done. A client that finds the echo disagreeing with what it asked has a server bug or a desync and must not write to the fd.
WHAT THE FD IS NOT. It is not a channel this protocol continues to mediate: once delivered, bytes travel between the principal and the far end through the proxy, and nothing in this document inspects them. Revocation kills the grant row and stops further request_connect immediately; whether it also closes THIS socket is the proxy's to do, and it can, because the proxy holds the other end - a property a delivered file descriptor does not share. No deployment does any of this today.
THE RAZOR. An event refuses nothing and this one is never an error. Its only fatal side is the client's, and it is the one-fd rule above.

arg.name: fd
arg.summary: the connected stream socket, owned by the receiving principal

arg.name: host
arg.summary: echo of the host this socket is connected to, byte-identical to the request's (max 253 bytes)

arg.name: port
arg.summary: echo of the port this socket is connected to

event.name: connect_failed

description.summary: an admitted request_connect that the far end did not answer

event.description:
Exactly one per failed request_connect, in request order, never coalesced, and it is a TERMINAL: the request is over, and no connected event follows.
THIS EVENT IS NEVER AN AUTHORITY ANSWER. Reaching it means the enforcement chokepoint ADMITTED the use - the grant is live, the verb is in the effective set, and the endpoint is covered - and the far end then did not answer. Every authority answer, and every failure of this server, is vitrin_grant.refused instead. A client that treats this event as a lost authority is wrong in the expensive direction: it will abandon work it is permitted to do.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THE reason ENUM: a proxy that is not running, not reachable, or that failed while setting the connection up. That is a failure of THIS server, so it voices vitrin_grant.refused(egress, internal) like every other server-side failure. The line this enum draws is the far end; anything on this side of it is the chokepoint's to answer.
There is no retry hint. vitrin_grant.refused carries retry_after_ms because a token bucket has a known refill time; a host that is down has none, and inventing one would be a number with nothing behind it. An agent's backoff is its own.
THE RAZOR. Recoverable, always, at every reason. The connection did not happen; the facet, the grant and the connection all stay exactly as they were, and the client may ask again.

arg.name: reason
arg.summary: what the far end did instead of answering

enum.name: failure

description.summary: why an admitted connection did not complete

enum.description:
Every entry names something that happened at or beyond the far end. Nothing here is a decision about a grant, and nothing here is a failure of this server - those are vitrin_grant.refusal's, and keeping the two enums disjoint is what lets a client route on the event type alone.
Values are immutable and entries append, like every other enum in this document; an out-of-range value is fatal "invalid_argument", so a deployment that meets a failure mode not listed here reports the closest listed one rather than inventing a value.
The set is deliberately COARSE. A finer taxonomy would be a finer description of the network the realm cannot otherwise see, and the grant's authority is to reach one endpoint rather than to survey the path to it. Four outcomes are what an agent's retry decision actually turns on.

entry.name: refused
entry.summary: the far end actively refused the connection (nothing listening on that port)

entry.name: unreachable
entry.summary: no route to the host or the network; the packet had nowhere to go

entry.name: timed_out
entry.summary: the connection attempt exceeded the proxy's deadline with no answer either way

entry.name: resolution_failed
entry.summary: the selector named a DNS name and resolution - which happens only in the proxy, never inside the realm - did not yield an address
